Surah al-Hadid

A group of narrators related from Ibn ʿAbbas that it was revealed in Medina. Al-Naqqash and others said: it is Medinan by the consensus of the exegetes (mufassirun). This was not accepted from him, for a people said it is Meccan. Indeed, the majority, as Ibn al-Faras said, hold this view.

Ibn ʿAtiyya said: there is no disagreement that it contains Medinan verses, but its beginning seems to be Meccan. This is supported by what al-Bazzar in his Musnad, al-Tabarani, Ibn Mardawayh, Abu Nuʿaym in al-Hilya, al-Bayhaqi and Ibn ʿAsakir related from ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with him, that he entered upon his sister before he embraced Islam, and there was a sheet (sahifa) containing the beginning of Surah al-Hadid. He read it until he reached ﴿Believe in Allah and His Messenger, and spend from that of which He has made you successors﴾ [al-Hadid: 7], and then he embraced Islam. And it is supported, for other Meccan verses, by what Muslim, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Majah and others related from Ibn Masʿud: "The time between our becoming Muslim and Allah reproaching us with this verse ﴿Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should humble themselves to the remembrance of Allah﴾ [al-Hadid: 16] was only four years." Al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and others related from ʿAbd Allah ibn al-Zubayr that Ibn Masʿud informed him that the time between their becoming Muslim and the revelation of this verse, by which Allah reproached them, was only four years: ﴿And do not be like those who were given the Scripture before, ...﴾ [al-Hadid: 16], the verse. However, there will come, if Allah wills, reports indicating the Medinan character of what was mentioned, and perhaps they are not fit to counter this.

It was revealed on Tuesday, according to what al-Daylami related from Jabir, raised to the Prophet: "Do not perform cupping on Tuesday, for Surah al-Hadid was revealed to me on Tuesday." Also in this matter there is a report that al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn ʿUmar, may Allah be pleased with both of them, with a weak chain. It has twenty-nine verses according to the Iraqi count, and twenty-eight according to others. Its connection to the preceding surah (al-Waqiʿa) is that it begins with mention of tasbih (glorification), and that surah ends with the command to it. Its opening stands in the place of the cause (ʿilla) for the command to it, as if it were said: (So glorify the name of your Lord, the Great) [al-Waqiʿa: 74, 96; al-Haqqa: 52], because whatever is in the heavens and the earth glorifies Him. As for its merit along with its sister surahs, there is what Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, al-Tirmidhi, who graded it as hasan, al-Nasa'i, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi in Shuʿab al-Iman related from ʿIrbad ibn Sariya: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to recite the musabbihat before he slept, and he said: 'Indeed, among them there is a verse better than a thousand verses.'" Ibn al-Darис related something similar from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir.

Then he said: Yahya said: "We consider it to be the verse at the end of al-Hashr."

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿Whatever is in the heavens and the earth exalts Allah﴾. Tasbih, according to the well-known view, is declaring Allah transcendent, in belief, speech and action, above what does not befit His majesty, glory be to Him. It derives from sabaha, meaning to go away and go far in water or land. Here He attributes it to non-rational beings as well, since "whatever is in the heavens and the earth" encompasses all that is in them, whether it is fixed within them or part of them. Rather, what is meant by "what is in them" is the existents (al-mawjudat), so this is more evident in covering the heavens and the earth, and it also covers the immaterial existents according to those who affirm them. The majority said: it is meant in a general, metaphorical sense, inclusive of what is expressed by the tongue of speech, such as the glorification of the angels and the believers among the two weighty ones (humans and jinn), and by the tongue of state (lisan al-hal), such as the glorification of others, for every individual of the existents indicates, by its contingency (imkan) and its origination (huduth), the Eternal Creator, the Necessarily Existent, characterized by every perfection and free from every deficiency. Some went to the view that tasbih is in its literal, well-known meaning for all things, and this is based on the affirmation of rational souls and of perception in all animals and inanimate things, each according to what befits it. A group of Sufis has explicitly stated this, so the glorification of everything, according to them, is speech, though the matter varies. It has also been said: the meaning of sabbaha is that he made his rational beholder (ra'iy) say "Subhan Allah" and drew his attention to it. But this, as you see, is weak. Whoever permits using a word in both its literal and metaphorical senses together does not need the generality of metaphor.

Al-Tabarsi permitted that what is meant (ma) is only the world (al-ʿalam), like the expression of the people of the Hijaz, as Abu Zayd related, upon hearing thunder: "Glory be to what You glorify." It is not hidden that its generality, covering the world and other than it, is preferable. Apparently, in both cases, ma is a relative pronoun (mawsula). Some said: it is an indefinite qualified noun (nakira mawsufa), and that the original sentence is "what is in the heavens and what is in the earth," then the second ma was deleted and its qualifier placed in its position. It is not good for it to be a relative pronoun, because according to the Basrans a relative clause does not stand in place of the relative pronoun, whereas a qualifier does stand in place of the qualified noun according to all. Relying on what is agreed upon is preferable to relying on what is disputed. That the mentioned one is a relative pronoun and the deleted one an indefinite qualified noun is a matter with no basis. End of quotation.

You know that deleting an explicit relative pronoun in such contexts is more than can be counted. The lam is used with tasbih, although tasbih is transitive by itself, as in His saying: ﴿and glorify Him﴾ [al-Fath: 9]. So it is extra (zaʾida) for emphasis, as in nasahtu lahu and shakartu lahu. It has also been said that it is for causation (li al-taʿlil), and the verb is treated as intransitive, meaning: he performed the tasbih and carried it out for the sake of Allah and sincerely for His Face, glory be to Him. There is something in this that is not hidden. The past tense is used here and in some of its sister surahs, and the present tense in others, to indicate the realization of tasbih at all times. In each there is an indication that it is the nature of what tasbih is attributed to that it glorifies Him, and that is its constant habit and practice. As for the indication of the present tense, it points to continuity up to the time of the report, and likewise in the time to come, because the meaning requires tasbih and the word is suited to that, since it is stripped of indication of time, and it is preferred over the noun to indicate the renewal of glorification after glorification. As for the indication of the past tense, it is also stripped of time, with the realization that it requires, so it covers the past time and the future time alike. It has been said: the indication and the showing of continuity are derived from both the past and present together, since the past indicates continuity up to the time of the report, and the present indicates continuity in the present and future, so together they cover all times. Al-Tibi said: some surahs open with a verbal noun (maṣdar), some with the past, some with the present, and some with the imperative. Thus all aspects of this word are comprehended, to make known that created beings, from their bringing out of non-existence into existence and onward to eternity, are glorifying and sanctifying His Essence, glory be to Him, exalted, in speech and deed, willingly and unwillingly. ﴿And there is not a thing but that it exalts [Allah] with His praise﴾ [al-Isra': 44].

﴿And He is the Mighty﴾: the Capable, the Dominant, whom nothing contests or prevents. ﴿the Wise﴾: who does only what wisdom and benefit require. The sentence is a parenthetical concluding statement (i'tiraḍ tadhyili) that confirms the content of what precedes it and indicates the reason for the ruling. Likewise His saying: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾, that is, the total disposal over them and over what is in them of existents, in terms of bringing into being and annihilation and all other dispositions. His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿He gives life and causes death﴾, that is, He performs giving life and causing death. It is a resumptive statement (istiʾnaf) explaining some of the rulings of the King. If it is taken as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning "He gives life and causes death," then that sentence is of this kind. Making it a circumstantial clause (ḥal) from the pronoun in lahu would imply restricting the King's exclusive authority to this state. His saying: ﴿And He is over all things﴾, among the things of which the giving of life and causing of death are part, ﴿competent﴾: emphatic in power. It is a concluding and completing statement for what precedes it.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 57, verse 3:**

﴿He is the First﴾: He who precedes all existent things. He, glorified is He, exists before everything, even before time, because He, majestic and exalted, is the one who brings into being and originates all existent things. ﴿And the Last﴾: He who remains after their annihilation, in reality, or in consideration of their essence when one sets aside their Sustainer. For all contingent existent things, if one sets aside their cause, are perishing.

From this, Ibn Sina (Avicenna) said: "The contingent, in its own essence, is nothing, and by its cause it is from non-existence." This does not contradict the fact that some contingent existent things do not perish, such as Paradise and Hell and those in them, as is established and clarified by the verses and the hadiths, because their perishing in its own essence is a matter that does not separate from them. It may be said: the perishing of every contingent thing in actuality is not observed, and what the proof indicates is only its contingency. So the "afterness" in such a case is according to imagination and estimation.

It has also been said: He is the First, from whom the causes begin, since He, glorified is He, is their Causer, and the Last, to whom the effects end. So the priority is essential, and the lastness means that He, exalted is He, is the place of return and the final destination, setting aside the permanence established by the proofs.

It has also been said: the First is in external reality, because He, exalted is He, brought things into being, so He, glorified is He, is prior to them in the external reality, and the Last is in the mind and in terms of relation, because He, mighty is His majesty, is inferred through the existent things that point to the eternal Creator, as it is said: "I have not seen anything except that I have seen God after it."

Hujjat al-Islam al-Ghazali said: The First is first in relation to something, and the Last is last in relation to something, and these two are contradictory. It is not conceivable that one thing, from one aspect, is first in relation to them, since all of them have derived existence from Him, glorified is He. As for Him, mighty and majestic is He, He exists by His essence, and He has not derived existence from another, glorified is He and exalted above that. And whatever you consider the order of the path and observe the stations of the wayfarers, He, exalted is He, is the Last, since He is the last that the degrees of the knowers ascend to, and every knowledge that is attained before the knowledge of Him, exalted is He, is ascended toward the knowledge of Him, majestic is He. The furthest station is the knowledge of Allah, majestic is His majesty. So He, glorified is He, is last in relation to the path, and first in relation to existence. From Him, mighty is His glory, is the origin at first, and to Him, glorified is He, is the return and the final destination, last. End of quotation.

It is apparent that His being First and Last in relation to existent things is more appropriate, and perhaps what he mentioned is more in harmony with the way of the people (the Sufis).

﴿And the Manifest﴾ (al-Zahir): that is, by His existence, since all existent things are manifest through His manifestation, exalted is He. ﴿And the Hidden﴾ (al-Batin): by His essence, glorified is He, so the intellects do not hover around Him.

Hujjat al-Islam said: These two attributes are relational, so a thing cannot be manifest to something and hidden to it from one aspect. Rather, it is manifest from one aspect in relation to a perception, and hidden from another aspect. Manifestness and hiddenness only occur in relation to perceptions. Allah, exalted is He, is hidden if sought through the perception of the senses and the storehouse of imagination, and manifest if sought through the storehouse of the intellect by inference. Doubt arises from extreme manifestness, and whatever exceeds its limit reverses into its opposite.

Al-Zamakhshari went to interpreting "the Hidden" as that which is not perceived by the senses. Then he said: The first waw (conjunction) is for coordinating a single term with a single term, so it indicates that He, exalted is He, combines the two attributes of priority and posteriority. The last (pair) is likewise, so it indicates that He, exalted is He, combines manifestness and concealment. As for the middle (waw), it is for coordinating a compound with a compound, so it indicates that He, majestic and exalted is He, combines the totality of the first two attributes and the totality of the latter two attributes. So He, exalted is He, is the one whose existence persists in all past and future times, and He, exalted is He, in all of them is manifest and hidden, combining manifestness through proofs and concealment, so He is not perceived by the senses. In this is a proof against the one who permits seeing Him, glorified is He, in the Hereafter by sight, that is: because He, exalted is He, there is no time in which it is correct to describe Him by priority and posteriority without it being correct to describe Him by manifestness and hiddenness together. So if one permits perceiving Him, glorified is He, by sight in the Hereafter, one has denied that He, glorified is He, is hidden, and this is contrary to what the verse indicates.

The author of al-Kashf answered this, saying: The interpretation of "the Hidden" as "not perceived by the senses" is an interpretation according to whim, since His being hidden from the perception of the intellects is like His being hidden from the perception of the senses, because the reality of the Essence is not perceived, neither by intellect nor by sense, by agreement among the verifiers of both groups. And al-Zamakhshari is among those who accept this. So He is the Manifest by His existence and the Hidden by His essence, and He, glorified is He, combines the two attributes eternally and everlastingly. This does not contradict the vision (of Allah), because it does not produce this according to its affirmers. End of quotation. And this is good, so do not be heedless.

Accordingly, the concluding phrase with His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And He is Knower of all things﴾ is to prevent the supposition that His being hidden from things entails that things are hidden from Him, majestic and exalted is He, as is the case among created beings.

Al-Azhari said: The manifest and the hidden may also be in the sense of knowledge, for what is manifest and hidden. That is because whoever is manifest is veiled from the hidden, and whoever is hidden is veiled from the manifest. So if you want to describe Him with knowledge, you say: He is the manifest and the hidden, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Neither of the east nor of the west﴾ [An-Nur: 35], that is, neither eastern only nor western only, but it is eastern and western. In the concluding phrase mentioned, then, there is obscurity. Close to this, from the aspect of what has been transmitted, is that the Manifest means the one exalted above everything, dominant over it, from His saying: "He prevailed over them" when he rose above them and overcame them. And the Hidden is the one who has known the inner reality of everything, that is, He knows its inner reality. It was objected that the correspondence between the manifest and the hidden is lost upon this, and that "batana" in the sense of "knew its inner reality" is not established in the language. However, it has been said regarding the reports: what supports the interpretation of the manifest by what has been interpreted.

Muslim, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, and al-Bayhaqi related on the authority of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, came to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) asking him for a servant. He said to her: Say: O Allah, Lord of the seven heavens and Lord of the Mighty Throne, our Lord and Lord of everything, Revealer of the Torah, the Gospel, and the Criterion, Splitter of the grain and the date-stone, I seek refuge in You from the evil of everything You hold by its forelock. You are the First, so nothing is before You, and You are the Last, so nothing is after You, and You are the Manifest, so nothing is above You, and You are the Hidden, so nothing is beneath You. Settle our debt for us and enrich us from poverty."

Al-Tibi said: The meaning of "the Manifest" in the prophetic interpretation is the Overpowering, who overcomes and is not overcome, and so disposes of the created beings by way of dominance and mastery, since there is no one above Him to prevent Him. And by "the Hidden" is meant the one beyond whom there is no refuge or shelter to which a seeker of refuge turns. It was examined on the possibility that the meaning is: You are the Manifest, so nothing is above You in manifestness, that is, You are more manifest than everything, since the manifestness of everything is through You. And You are the Hidden, so nothing is beneath You in hiddenness, that is, You are more hidden than everything, since everything's reality is known by other than it, and You are that, and You are not known in reality by other than You. Or because everything can have its reality known, but You cannot be known in reality at all. Also, in the indication of "the Hidden" upon what he said there is great obscurity. Moreover, if the matter were as mentioned, the eminent scholars would not have turned away from it, since the report is authentic. Something similar has come from the narrations of Imam Ahmad, Abu Dawud, and Ibn Majah. It is far-fetched that these eminent scholars did not come across it. Even more far-fetched is that what the Prophet (ﷺ) mentioned of the Divine Names is other than what is in the verse. It is possible that the Prophet (ﷺ), upon peace and blessings, meant by his saying: "so nothing is beneath You" that nothing is closer to You. This is supported by what al-Bayhaqi in al-Asma' wa al-Sifat related on the authority of Muqatil, who said: "It has reached us regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He is the First﴾ etc.: He is the First before everything, the Last after everything, the Manifest above everything, and the Hidden closer than everything." And He only means nearness by His knowledge and power, and He is above His Throne. What is most preponderant to me is what was mentioned first.

Regarding some Sufis who held the doctrine of the Unity of Existence (wahdat al-wujud), they held that the meaning of His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He is the First﴾ etc. is that there is no existent other than Him, exalted is He, since everything that is conceived as existent is either first or last, and He, glorified is He, alone is that, not other than Him. They supported this with what is in a raised (marfu') hadith related by Imam Ahmad, Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn al-Mundhir, and a group, on the authority of Abu Hurayrah: "By Him in whose hand is my soul, if you were lowered with a rope into the lowest earth, it would descend upon Allah." Abu Hurayrah said: Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿He is the First and the Last and the Manifest and the Hidden, and He is Knower of all things﴾.

The doctrine of the Unity of Existence is well known. As for the report, it is among the ambiguous (mutashabih) texts. Al-Tirmidhi said regarding it: The people of knowledge have interpreted the hadith, saying: that is, it would descend upon the knowledge of Allah, His power, and His dominion. This is supported by the mention of the concluding phrase and his (ﷺ) not confining it to what came before it. This verse should be recited by whoever finds in himself a whispered doubt concerning Allah, exalted is He. Abu Dawud related on the authority of Abu Zumayl that Ibn Abbas said to him, when he informed him that he had a whisper regarding that: "When you find something in yourself, say: He is the First," and the verse.

Abu al-Shaykh related in al-Azamah on the authority of Ibn Umar and Abu Sa'id, may Allah be pleased with them, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "People will not cease asking about everything until they say: This is Allah; He was before everything. Then what was before Allah? If they say that to you, then say: He is the First, the Last, the Manifest, and the Hidden, and He is Knower of all things."

He it is who created the heavens and the earth in six days, then established Himself upon the Throne. This explains some of the rulings concerning His dominion over them, and its tafsir (interpretation) has been covered several times. ﴿He knows what enters into the earth and what comes out of it, and what descends from the heaven and what ascends into it.﴾ Its explanation has already passed in Surah Saba'. ﴿And He is with you wherever you are.﴾ This is a figure of speech for the comprehensiveness of His knowledge of them, and a depiction that they cannot escape it wherever they are. It has been said that "being with" (al-ma'iyyah) is a metonymy (majaz mursal) for knowledge, through the relation of causation, and the indicator is the context of what precedes and follows, along with the impossibility of the literal meaning. The early generation (al-salaf) interpreted this verse in this way. Al-Bayhaqi, in al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat, transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding it: "He is knowing of you wherever you are."

He also transmitted from Sufyan al-Thawri that he was asked about it and said: "His knowledge is with you." In al-Bahr (al-Bahr al-Muhit, the Ocean) it is stated that the community (al-ummah) has agreed upon this interpretation of it, and that it is not to be taken in its apparent sense of being-with in essence. This is evidence against prohibiting ta'wil (figurative interpretation) in other verses that are similar to it in the impossibility of taking them literally. He interpreted this verse, and interpreted the Black Stone as "the right hand of God on earth." Had his intellect been broader, he would have interpreted other things of the same meaning, to the end.

You know that the safer course is to abandon ta'wil, for it is speaking about God without knowledge. We interpret only what the early generation interpreted, and we follow them in what they were upon. If they interpreted, we interpret; if they committed the matter to God (tafwid), we commit it. We do not take their interpretation of something as a basis for accepting the interpretation of others. I have seen some of the zindiqs (heretics) who have left the noose of Islam laughing at this verse together with His saying, ﴿then established Himself upon the Throne﴾, and mocking the Noble Qur'an for it. This is a monstrous ignorance and an appalling disbelief. We ask God, exalted is He, for protection and success.

﴿And God is Seeing of what you do.﴾ This is an expression of His encompassing of their deeds. The mention of the attribute of knowledge, which is among the attributes of His essence (sifat al-dhat), is placed after the creation, which is among the attributes of actions (sifat al-af'al), even though the attributes of essence precede the attributes of actions, because the intended meaning is to point to the knowledge upon which the recompense depends, which follows the known object. It has also been said that creation is evidence of knowledge, since by His creation and His bringing into existence of His perfectly crafted creatures one can infer that He, mighty and majestic, is knowing. The derived thing (al-madlul) must necessarily come after the indicator (al-dalil), since it depends on it.

Al-Alusi, Ruh al-Ma'ani, on Surah 57, verse 5:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ is a repetition for emphasis and a preparation for His saying, exalted is He, which implies a return: ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾. That is, to Him alone, exalted is He, and not to anyone else, either independently or jointly, all matters are returned, both their accidents and their substances. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and al-A'raj read "tarji'" with the verb in the active voice, from raja'a, ruju'an. In the passive voice, as in the reading of the majority, it is from raja'a, raj'an.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 57, verse 6:

﴿He causes the night to enter into the day, and He causes the day to enter into the night﴾. Its interpretation has passed several times. And His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And He is Knowing﴾, that is, Exceedingly Knowing, ﴿of what is within the breasts﴾, that is, of what they conceal therein.

Page 169

The necessary matters attached to it are an explanation of the comprehensiveness of His knowledge, Exalted is He, of what they conceal of their intentions, after the explanation of His comprehensiveness of their deeds which they display. It is also permitted that ( of what is within the breasts ) means the breasts themselves and their reality, such that comprehensive knowledge of what is in them is known a fortiori.

Believe in God and His Messenger, and spend of that which He has made you successors (mustakhlafin) in. [Qur'an 57:7]

That is, He, glory be to Him, has made you successors (khulafa') of Him, exalted and majestic is He, in disposing of it, without your actually owning it. He, majestic is His station, expressed what is in their hands of wealth in this way, to affirm the truth and to encourage spending. For whoever knows that it belongs to God, Exalted is He, and that he is merely like a trustee who disburses it to the purposes God has specified, spending becomes easy for him. Or [the meaning is] that He has made you successors of those who came before you in what was in their hands, so it has passed on to you. In this there is also encouragement to spend and facilitation of it, because whoever knows that it has not remained with the one before him and has passed on to him, knows that it will not last for him and will pass on to someone else; so giving it out becomes easy for him, and he desires to earn reward through spending it. The saying of people about what you possessed suffices as a reminder: "This was once so-and-so's." And in the hadith: "The son of Adam says: 'My wealth, my wealth.' Do you have any wealth other than what you have eaten and so consumed, or worn and so worn out, or given in charity and so sent ahead?" The first meaning is the one that fits the words of God, Exalted: ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾. And in line with it is what is related: it was said to a Bedouin, "To whom do these camels belong?" He said, "They belong to God, Exalted, in my view." And the verse of the poet inclines toward it:

"Wealth and family are only deposits, and deposits must one day be returned."

And the verse, according to what is related from al-Dahhak, was revealed concerning Tabuk, so do not be heedless. ﴿Then those of you who believe and spend﴾ as they were commanded, ﴿for them﴾ by reason of that ﴿is a great reward﴾. This is a promise containing emphasis that is not hidden, in that He made the sentence a nominal one, whereas the apparent form, in response to a command, would have been verbal, saying for instance: "Believe in God and His Messenger and spend, you will be given a great reward." The belief and the spending are mentioned again rather than saying "whoever does that, for him is a great reward," and He turned away from "for those who believe among you and spend, there is a reward" toward what is in the noble composition. The reward is made emphatic by being indefinite, and it is described as great.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 57, verse 8:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe in Allah?﴾ is a resumptive clause (istinaf). It is said that it is brought to rebuke them for abandoning faith, as they were commanded, by denying that they have any excuse whatsoever for it. The phrase "that you do not believe" is a circumstantial clause (hal) referring to the pronoun in "lakum" (for you), and the element governing it is the sense of stability contained within the preposition (al-istiqrar). The meaning is: "What has happened to you while not believing?" This directs the denial and negation only at the cause, while affirming the effect, namely the content of the circumstantial clause, which is the absence of faith. Thus the denial is aimed only at the existing cause and its negation. A parallel to this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What is [the matter] with you that you do not expect dignity from Allah?﴾ (Nuh 13). The denial and negation may also be directed at the cause of an occurrence in this kind of construction, so that they extend to the effect as well, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And why should I not worship...﴾ (Ya-Sin 22), etc. This cannot be applied here, because the absence of faith is established. This meaning is free of any objection.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while the Messenger calls you to believe in your Lord﴾ is a circumstantial clause referring to the pronoun in "do not believe". It conveys, as has been said, a rebuke for their disbelief, given that what necessitates their faith exists, after rebuking them for its absence despite what necessitates it. The lam in "li-tu'minu" (that you may believe) is connected to "yad'u" (calls), which takes it as well as "ila" (to). That is: "And what excuse do you have for abandoning faith, while the Messenger calls you [to it] and reminds you of it?" It is also permissible for the lam to be causal (ta'liliyyah).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He has already taken your covenant﴾ is a circumstantial clause referring either to the subject of "yad'u" (calls) or to its object. That is: "And Allah has already taken your covenant to believe, from before", as the difference between the two verbs, one in the present and one in the past, indicates. It is also permissible for it to be a circumstantial clause conjoined to the preceding circumstantial clause, so that the clause is a circumstantial clause following another circumstantial clause, referring to the pronoun in (you believe). The difference between the nominal and the verbal form makes this less likely in general.

In any case, the "taking of the covenant" refers to what came from Him, exalted is He, in establishing the signs of the horizons and of the souls,
[p. 170]
and in enabling reflection. So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while the Messenger calls you﴾ refers to the revealed (sam'i) proof, and this refers to the rational (aqli) proof. In the order of mention and delay there is support for the view that the revealed proof is more honourable than the rational proof.

Al-Baghawi said: "It is what happened when He brought them out from the loins of Adam and made them bear witness that He, glorified is He, is their Lord, and they bore witness." According to this view there is no metaphor. The first view is the one preferred by al-Zamakhshari. Ibn al-Munir criticised it, saying: "There is no objection to taking the covenant in its literal sense, which is what was taken on the Day of the Dharr (the primordial covenant of souls). Whatever reason permits and the Sharia has brought, it is obligatory to believe in." This was narrated from Mujahid, Ata', al-Kalbi and Muqatil. The Imam criticised it, saying: "The purpose is to obligate those addressed to believe and to deny that they have any excuse for abandoning it. They only know of this covenant through the Messenger. Before affirming the Messenger, it cannot be a reason for obligating them to believe in him." Al-Tibi said: "It is possible to say that if the pronoun in (took) refers to Allah, it is appropriate that the covenant means what is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿We said: Go down from it, all of you. Then when guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance...﴾ (al-Baqarah 38), etc., because the meaning is: 'If guidance comes to you from Me, by a messenger whom I send to you and a Book which I send down upon you.' The first is indicated by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿while the Messenger calls you to believe﴾, and the second by ﴿It is He who sends down upon His servant clear signs﴾, etc. If it refers to the Messenger, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, then the apparent meaning is what is in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [mention] when Allah took the covenant of the prophets: 'Whatever I give you of Book and wisdom, and then there comes to you a messenger confirming what is with you, you must believe in him and support him'﴾ (Al 'Imran 81), with the covenant being attributed to the prophets as the attribution of the one who makes the covenant binding, not the one bound by it. That is, the covenant which the prophets bound upon their nations. This is the preferred view, because the address is to the Companions, may Allah be pleased with them, as what follows indicates. Perhaps the covenant is like what we have narrated from Imam Ahmad, from Ubadah ibn al-Samit: 'The Messenger of Allah, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, took our pledge to hear and obey, in ease and in hardship, in spending in hardship and in ease, to enjoin good and forbid evil, and to speak the truth for Allah wherever we are, not fearing the blame of any blamer.' End of quotation."

The first view is weakened by the same argument the Imam used against interpreting the covenant as what took place on the Day of the Dharr. The weakness of the second is too evident to need pointing out.

Regarding the address, the author of al-Kashf said: "It is general, rebuking whoever among them did not believe for not believing, and then rebuking whoever did believe for not spending in His way."

The words of Abu Hayyan clearly indicate that it is addressed to the believers. He took "āminū" (believe) as a command to remain steadfast in faith and persist in it, and "what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe" as meaning: "How is it that you do not remain steadfast in faith, when the motives for it are present?"

The apparent meaning of some scholars' words is that it is addressed to the disbelievers, which is what we indicated earlier. Perhaps what the author of al-Kashf mentioned is preferable. However, it has been objected to it that if "āminū" is an address to those characterised by faith and to those not so characterised, this requires using the command to seek the very act for those not characterised by faith, and to seek steadfastness for those characterised by it. There is much to be said about this. To escape this difficulty, one would need to intend a general meaning covering both commands. It may be said that he intended that he addressed groups differing in their conditions, so they were given different commands and addressed with various addresses, and each command and address was directed to the one fitting for it. This is like a governor saying to the people of his city: "Call the adhan, pray, teach, spend on the poor, and give full measure and weight," and so on, since each command applies to those among them who are fitting for it. So reflect.

It was also read: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe in Allah and His Messenger?﴾ Abu 'Amr read (and His covenant has already been taken from you) in the passive voice, with "mithaqukum" (your covenant) in the nominative.

﴿if you are believers﴾ is a conditional clause whose response is omitted, indicated by what precedes it. The meaning is: "If you are believers by a cause of any kind, then this is a cause, and there is no cause beyond it." It is also permissible that the intended meaning is: "If you are among those who believe, then what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe, while in this state?" Al-Wahidi said: "That is, if you are believers by rational or transmitted proof, then it has become clear and manifest to you through Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, through his mission and the sending down of the Qur'an upon him." In any case, there is no contradiction between this and His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what is [the matter] with you that you do not believe?﴾

Al-Tabari said in this regard:
[p. 171]
"The meaning is: If you are believers in any state whatsoever, then believe now." It has also been said: "The meaning is: If you are believers in Musa and Isa, peace be upon them both, then believe in Muhammad, may Allah's blessings and peace be upon him, for their law requires faith in him, upon him be blessings and peace; or: If you are believers in the covenant taken from you in the world of the Dharr, then believe now." It has also been said: "The meaning is: If you remain upon faith, then you are in noble ranks and exalted stations." All of these, as you see, are far-fetched.

The apparent meaning of the last view is that the address is to the believers, and this is the one chosen by al-Tibi. Regarding this condition he said: "It may be taken as a conditional of cause (ta'lil), as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who believe, fear Allah and give up what remains of interest, if you are believers﴾ (al-Baqarah 278), because the speech with the believers is in the manner of rebuke and reproach, as what follows indicates."

He it is who sends down upon His servant, ﴿He it is who sends down upon His servant﴾ as much as He sees fit, according to the benefits that occur to you, ﴿clear signs﴾ that are evident. The apparent meaning is that by them are meant the verses of the Qur'an, though it has been said that they are the miracles (mu'jizat). ﴿That He may bring you out﴾, i.e., Allah, Exalted is He, since He is the one spoken of, or the servant, because of the proximity of mention. The intended meaning is "that He may bring you out by them" ﴿from the darknesses to the light﴾, from the darknesses of disbelief to the light of faith. It was read in the seven canonical readings (al-Sab'ah) as the present tense يُنَزِّلُ (yunazzilu), and some readers doubled the letter zay (tathqil) while others did not (takhfif).

al-Hasan read it both ways. Zayd ibn 'Ali and al-A'mash read أَنْزَلَ (anzala) in the past tense. ﴿Indeed Allah is, toward you, Most Kind and Merciful﴾, exceeding in kindness (ra'fah) and mercy (rahmah), in that He removed from you the obstacles to the happiness of both abodes and guided you to it in the most complete manner. It was read in the seven canonical readings as لَرَؤُوفٌ (la-ra'uf) with two waws,

The Qur'anic phrase ﴿وما لَكم ألا تُنْفِقُوا﴾ is a rebuke for not spending. It may address the believers who do not spend, or those first rebuked for not believing. Allah, glory be to Him, rebukes them for this after rebuking them for not believing, by denying that they have any excuse for it either. The word (أنْ) is a verbal (maṣdariyyah) particle, not an extra (zā'idah) one as some have said. This is the view implied by the words of al-Akhfash (al-Akhfash al-Awsat). The clause is in the position of an object after the omitted preposition, so the verbal noun phrase is in the accusative or genitive position according to the two views. The object of "spending" is omitted because it is known from what preceded. The words ﴿فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ﴾ (in the way of Allah) intensify the rebuke. What is meant is every good that brings them closer to Him, by way of explicit metaphor (al-istiʿārah al-taṣrīḥiyyah). The sense is: what is the matter with you, that you do not spend in what brings you nearer to Allah, the Exalted, when it truly belongs to Him? You are only His stewards in disposing of it to the uses He has designated, or of what has passed to you from others and will pass from you to others.

﴿ولِلَّهِ مِيراثُ السَّماواتِ والأرْضِ﴾ means: He inherits everything in them, and no one retains any property. The inheritance of the heavens and the earth is either metaphorical or a metonymy for the inheritance of what is in them, because taking possession of the container entails taking possession of what is contained.

It is also permitted that the meaning be that He inherits them and what is in them. The first view is preferred, because it suffices for the rebuke, since the heavens and earth have no connection here to being taken. The sentence is a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the subject of "do not spend" or from its object. It emphasises the rebuke, for withholding spending without cause is ugly and reprehensible. When the reasons that require spending are present, it is even uglier and more clearly denounced. The statement that all the wealth in the heavens and the earth will remain to Allah, the Exalted, in the Hereafter, with no one of its owners retaining anything, is stronger in requiring spending than the statement that it truly belongs to Him, or that it has passed to them from others. It is as if it were said: What is the matter with you, in withholding its spending in the way of Allah, the Exalted, when neither you nor others will retain any of it, but all of it will remain to Allah, the Exalted? Stating the glorious Name in place of a pronoun serves to add confirmation and to inspire awe.

The words ﴿لا يَسْتَوِي مِنكم مَن أنْفَقَ مَن قَبْلِ الفَتْحِ وقاتَلَ﴾ (Not equal among you are those who spent before the victory and fought) explain the differences in rank among the spenders according to the differences in their circumstances in spending, after stating that they have a great reward in absolute terms. This urges them to seek the best. The conjunction of fighting with spending indicates that fighting is one of the most important sources of spending, and that it is in itself one of the best acts of worship, and that it is never free of spending altogether. The counterpart of ﴿مَن أنْفَقَ﴾ is omitted, meaning: that is not equal to others. It is omitted because it is evident and because what follows indicates it. The "victory" (al-fatḥ) is the conquest of Makkah according to what is reported from Qatadah, Zayd ibn Aslam and Mujahid, and this is the well-known view. Its definiteness is either for a specific reference or for a generic sense by way of claim. Al-Sha'bi said it is the victory of al-Hudaybiyyah. The reason it is called a victory has already been discussed in the commentary on Surah al-Fath, and some reports indicate this.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym, in al-Dala'il, related through Zayd ibn Aslam, from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "We went out with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the year of al-Hudaybiyyah. When we reached 'Usfan, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Soon a people will come who will look down upon your deeds in comparison with their deeds.' We said: 'Who are they, O Messenger of Allah? Are they Quraysh?' He said: 'No, but they are the people of Yemen. They are gentler of heart and softer of hearts.' We said: 'Are they better than us, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'If one of them had a mountain of gold and spent it, he would not reach the mudd of one of you, nor half of it. Behold, this is the distinction between us and the people.'" Then the verse: ﴿لا يَسْتَوِي مِنكم مَن أنْفَقَ مَن قَبْلِ الفَتْحِ﴾ and so on.

Zayd ibn ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with both of them, read "qabl" (قَبْلَ) without "min" (مِن). The demonstrative ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ (those) refers to "those who spent". The plural is according to the meaning of "man" (مَن), just as the singular of the two preceding pronouns is according to its wording. The use of the distant demonstrative in place of a pronoun serves to glorify them and to signal that the basis of the ruling is their spending before the victory and their fighting. Its position is nominative, as the subject (mubtadaʾ), and the predicate is the words ﴿أعْظَمُ دَرَجَةً﴾ (are greater in rank), meaning: those described by these two noble qualities are higher in station and greater in standing.

﴿مِنَ الَّذِينَ أنْفَقُوا مِنَ بَعْدُ﴾ (than those who spent afterwards) means after the victory, ﴿وقاتَلُوا﴾ (and fought). Some have held that the subject of "is not equal" (لا يَسْتَوِي) is a pronoun referring to "spending", meaning: spending itself is not equal, that is, its kind, since some of it is before the victory and some after it. In this reading "those who spent" (مَن أنْفَقَ) is a subject, and the clause ﴿أُولَئِكَ أعْظَمُ﴾ is its predicate. This involves breaking up the speech and departing from its apparent sense without a compelling reason, so the preferred reading is the earlier one. It is implicitly understood from it that there is a difference between spending before the victory and spending after it. Those who spent before were greater in rank than those who spent afterwards because they acted at a time of the greatest need for support with their lives and wealth, when Muslims were few, their enemies many, and there were none of the things that souls naturally desire, such as abundant spoils. That made their deed more beneficial and more burdensome to the self. Its doer has stronger certainty in what is with Allah, the Exalted, and greater desire for it. This is not so for those who spent afterwards.

The word ﴿وكُلّا﴾ (and to each) means each of the two groups, not only the first two. ﴿وعَدَ اللَّهُ الحُسْنى﴾ (Allah has promised the best) means the best reward, which is Paradise according to what is reported from Mujahid and Qatadah. It is said that it is more general than this, including victory and spoils in this world. Ibn ʿĀmir and ʿAbd al-Warith read "wa-kullun" (وكُلٌّ) with a nominative ending. The apparent view is that it is a subject (mubtadaʾ), and the sentence after it is its predicate, with an omitted returning pronoun, meaning: "His promise". This is like the line of poetry:

"And Khalid is praised, our masters, in truth, and is not praised in falsehood."

The meaning is: "praises him". The sentence is coordinated with ﴿أُولَئِكَ أعْظَمُ دَرَجَةً﴾, and between them there is a correspondence that is absent in the reading of the majority. The Basrans prohibited omitting the returning pronoun from the predicate of a subject, and said it is permitted only in poetry, unlike omitting it from a relative clause. They are refuted by this reading. The view of some of them about it, that "kullun" is the predicate of a subject whose estimated form is "wa-ulā'ika kullun", with the clause "Allah has promised" as a descriptive clause of "kullun", is a weak interpretation, and it involves additional omission. Moreover, some grammarians prohibited describing "kullun" with a clause, because it is definite by being estimated as "wa-kulluhum" (and all of them). Al-Shihab said: The correct view is that of Ibn Malik, that the omission of a returning pronoun from a predicate clause is not permitted except in "kullun" and what resembles it in needing a referent and in generality. In that case it is regular, but the consensus (ijmāʿ) has been claimed for it, and that is a point of dispute.

﴿واللَّهُ بِما تَعْمَلُونَ خَبِيرٌ﴾ (And Allah is Aware of what you do) means He knows its outward and inward aspects and will recompense you according to it. The speech thus contains both promise and warning. In these verses there is evidence of the excellence of the foremost emigrants and the Helpers, which is clear. What is meant by them is the believers who spent and fought before the conquest of Makkah, or before al-Hudaybiyyah, according to the earlier difference. The verse, as al-Wahidi related from al-Kalbi, was revealed concerning Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may Allah be pleased with him, meaning because of him. You know that the specificity of the occasion does not indicate the specificity of the ruling, which is why it said ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ so as to include others than him, may Allah be pleased with him, who share this quality. Yes, he is the most complete of them, for he spent all his wealth before the conquest and before the Hijrah, and gave his own self along with it, upon him be blessings and peace. For this reason the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "No one has been more generous to me in his companionship than Abu Bakr." That suffices for the revelation to be concerning him.

In al-Kashshaf it is said that ﴿أُولَئِكَ﴾ are the foremost first among the emigrants and Helpers, about whom the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "If one of you spent the equivalent of Uhud in gold, he would not reach the mudd of one of them, nor half of it." Al-Tayyibi said: The hadith is from the narrations of al-Bukhari, Muslim, Abu Dawud and al-Tirmidhi, from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Do not revile my Companions. Even if one of you spent the equivalent of Uhud in gold, he would not reach the mudd of one of them, nor half of it." Al-Kashf criticised this, saying that on this view it is not restricted to the foremost first, as al-Kashshaf indicated. This is based on the premise that the address in "do not revile" is not to those present or those living in his time (ﷺ), but to everyone who is fit to be addressed, as in the words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿ولَوْ تَرى إذْ وُقِفُوا﴾ [al-An'am: 27, 30] and so on. Otherwise, it has been said that address requires presence and existence, and there must be a difference between the addressed and those forbidden to revile them. Thus they are the foremost, the perfect in companionship.

I say: The use of this hadith as evidence for the excellence of the Companions in general has spread, on the basis of the claim that the plural construct (iḍāfat al-jam') conveys comprehensiveness. Al-Kashf holds this view. The matter of the address has been raised as a difficulty, and it has been answered with what you have heard, and also by saying that it is in the manner of the eternal address of Allah, the Exalted. However, some reports support that those addressed are some of the Companions and those praised are another part of them, so the construct would be for a specific reference, or by taking "the Companions" to mean the perfect in companionship.

Al-Ahmad related from Anas, who said: "There was a dispute between Khalid ibn al-Walid and ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf. Khalid said to ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn ʿAwf: 'You consider yourselves superior to us because of days that you preceded us in.' This reached the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: 'Leave my Companions to me. By the One in whose hand is my soul, if you spent the equivalent of Uhud, or the equivalent of the mountains, in gold, you would not reach their deeds.'" Then in this hadith there is support for the view that those are the ones who spent before al-Hudaybiyyah, because his Islam (may Allah be pleased with him) was between al-Hudaybiyyah and the conquest of Makkah, as in al-Taqrib and elsewhere. Al-Zamakhshari interpreted the victory as the conquest of Makkah, so do not be heedless. Jalal al-Din al-Mahalli said: The address in "do not revile" is to the Companions who revile, and he said: The Prophet (ﷺ) treated them, through their reviling, which does not befit them, in a station other than theirs, since the reason given is what he mentioned. This is a good view, so reflect on it.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 57, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Who is it that will lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾ is an eloquent exhortation from Allah, exalted is He, to spend in His cause, reinforcing the earlier command to do so and rebuking those who neglect it. The interrogative is therefore not meant literally but serves to urge (al-hathth). The "goodly loan" (al-qard al-hasan) is spending with sincerity and seeking out the most noble wealth and the best channels. Some scholars have mentioned that the goodly loan comprises ten qualities:

That it be from lawful (halal) wealth, for Allah, exalted is He, is good and accepts only what is good.
That it be from the most noble of what a person possesses.
That it be given while the person is healthy and miserly, hoping to live and fearing poverty.
That he place it with the most needy and most deserving.
That he conceal it.
That he not follow it with reminders (al-mann) or harm (al-adha).
That he intend by it the Face of Allah, exalted is He.
That he consider little what he gives, even if it is much.
That it be from his most beloved wealth.
That he choose for delivering it to the poor the means that is most pleasing to him, such as carrying it to his home.

It should not be overlooked that these points may be increased or decreased.

Whichever is the case, the statement is either a figurative use in the verb, making it a metaphor in the verb form (istiʿarah tabiʿiyyah tasrihiyyah), or a figurative use in the whole sentence, making it an allegorical metaphor (istiʿarah tamthiliyyah), and this is the more eloquent. That is: who is it that spends his wealth in the cause of Allah, exalted is He, sincerely, seeking out its most noble and best channels, hoping that He, glorified is He, will replace it for him, as one who lends to Him, ﴿so that He may multiply it for him﴾, that is, give him his reward for his spending multiplied many times over by His bounty.

﴿And for him is a noble reward﴾: that is, that reward added to the multiplication is noble, pleasing in itself, worthy that competitors should compete for it. This indicates that the reward, just as it is increased in quantity, is also profound in quality. The clause is therefore circumstantial (ḥāliyyah), not coordinated with (﴿fa-yuḍāʿifahu﴾). It has been permitted to take it as coordinated, and the distinction holds between the multiplication and the reward itself, for the multiplication is pure bounty, and the equivalent is itself a bounty that is a reward.

The verb ﴿yuḍāʿifahu﴾ is in the subjunctive (naṣb) as an answer to the interrogative according to its meaning, as if it had been said: "Will anyone lend to Allah, exalted is He, so that He multiplies it for him?" For what is asked about, according to the wording, is the agent, though in meaning it is the act itself. The intent is not that the act has occurred and the question concerns the identity of its agent, as when you say, "Who came to you today?" after knowing that someone came to you without knowing him by name. Rather, this style is employed for emphasis in seeking, to the point that the act, because of the strength of its motives, seems to have already occurred, and one asks about its agent only in order to reward him. The apparent form was not taken into account, because it is agreed without dispute that the subjunctive after the fāʾ requires that what precedes it not contain the occurrence of the act, as in "Why did you strike Zayd, so that he repays you?", for in that case it does not contain the prior occurrence of a future verbal noun. On this basis every subjunctive construction is interpreted, where what precedes contains the occurrence.

Some readers recited ﴿fa-yuḍāʿifuhu﴾ with the indicative (rafʿ), according to the regular rule, considering the apparent sense which implies occurrence. It is either coordinated with ﴿yuqriḍu﴾ or with ﴿fahuwa (yuḍāʿifuhu)﴾. It has also been read as ﴿fa-yuḍʿifahu﴾ in both the indicative and the subjunctive.
