Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 57, verse 18:

﴿Indeed, the male givers of charity (al-musaddiqin) and the female givers of charity (al-musaddiqat)﴾, i.e., al-mutasaddiqin and al-mutasaddiqat. Ubayy also recited it thus. Ibn Kathir, Abu Bakr, al-Mufaddal, Aban, and Abu 'Amr, in the narration of Harun, recited it with the sad pronounced lightly (takhfif), from at-tasdiq (affirmation/belief), not from as-sadaqah (charity), as in the recitation of the majority (al-Jumhur). That is: those who affirmed (sadaqu) Allah, Mighty and Majestic, and His Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace; and the women who affirmed (sadaqna). The first recitation is more fitting with His words, Exalted is He: ﴿and lend to Allah a goodly loan﴾. It was said: the second is more preferred, because lending (al-iqrad) renders the mention of affirmation (tasdiq) unnecessary; and you will know, if Allah the Exalted wills, its benefit. The phrase ( "and lend" ) is conjoined to the sense of the verb within "al-musaddiqin," according to what Abu 'Ali and az-Zamakhshari chose, because "al" is in the sense of "alladhina" (those who), and the active participle is in the sense of a verb; so it is as if it were said: "Indeed those who gave charity or affirmed, according to the two recitations, and lent."
Page 182
Abu Hayyan and others criticized this, saying that it involves separating the parts of the relative clause (sila), since what is conjoined to the relative clause is "al-musaddiqat," which is a foreign element, and that is not permissible. The author of at-Taqrib said: it is to be understood according to the sense, as if it were said: "Indeed the people who gave charity, men and women, have lent," so it is a conjunction to the relative clause in meaning, without separation. This was criticized on the grounds that it has no real basis unless it is said that the second "al" is superfluous, so as not to conjoin to the form of part of a word; and this is far-fetched. It is not hidden that the principle of considering the meaning removes what has been mentioned. For this reason it was said: it is close, and it is not far to apply what preceded from Abu 'Ali and az-Zamakhshari to it. It was also said: the conjunction is to the relative "al" in "al-musaddiqat," and the variation of pronouns in feminine and masculine does no harm, because "al" is suitable for all, so it is meant by it the sense of "allati" (the feminine plural) when the feminine plural pronoun returns to it, and the sense of "alladhi" when the masculine plural pronoun returns to it. This, as you see, is [weak]. Similar to it is what was said: it is of the type of "kull rajul wa day'atahu" (every man and his household), i.e., the male and female givers of charity are coupled together in reward and station. Or a predicate may be supplied, i.e.: "Indeed the male and female givers of charity will prosper," and "and lend" in both cases is not a conjunction to the relative clause, but is resumptive (mustanaf), and it may be added after the adjective "qardan" or a resumption. Whoever is just does not see that this is something that should be applied to the speech of the least of the eloquent, let alone the speech of the Lord of the worlds. Abu Hayyan preferred to explain it as the deletion of the relative pronoun, since what precedes indicates it, as if it were said: "And those who lent," so it would be like his saying:

"Whoever among you abandons the Messenger of Allah, and praises him and supports him, is equal [to one who does not]."

This is acceptable according to the opinion of the Kufans, but not according to the opinion of the Basrans, for they do not permit the deletion of the relative pronoun in such a case. Some of the leading verifiers, after considering the explanation of at-Taqrib to be plausible, and not deeming far the application of what you heard from az-Zamakhshari and Abu 'Ali to it, said: "Closer to it is to say that (al-musaddiqat) is in the accusative by way of specification (takhsis), as if it were said: 'Indeed the male givers of charity' in a general sense by way of predominance (taghlib), and I specify the female givers of charity from among them, just as you say: 'Indeed those who believed, especially the scholars among them, and did righteous deeds, for them is such-and-such.'"

The reason for the specification is what has come in the saying of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace: "O assembly of women, give charity, for I have been shown that most of the people of the Fire are you," encouraging them to charity, that when they do so, it is more pleasing to Him, Exalted is He, and its reward from Him, glorified is He, is greater and more excellent. Then he said: Since lending is nothing other than that giving of charity, it is said: "and lent," i.e., by that giving of charity, to establish its reality, and that they are like that, being likened before Allah, Exalted is He, to one who deals with the best of the two bests, dealing in His pleasure. Had it been said "wal-muqridin" (the male and female lenders), this subtlety would have been lost. End.

It is not hidden that the accusative of "al-musaddiqat" by way of specification is contrary to the apparent sense. As for what he mentioned concerning the subtlety of diverting from the two assumed forms, it is good, and it is achieved according to the explanations of Abu 'Ali and az-Zamakhshari, and according to the explanation of Abu Hayyan. Al-Khafaji said: the statement of Abu al-Baqa' that "an aqradu" etc. is an interjection between the subject of "inna" and its predicate, which is more evident and easier. It seems the subtlety in it is the emphasis of the ruling by doubling, and he claimed that the clause is a circumstantial clause (hal), with "qad" implied or not, from the two pronouns of "al-musaddiqin" and "al-musaddiqat," which is not hidden in meaning or Arabic, so reflect. ﴿It is multiplied for them﴾: the pronoun refers to all the preceding men and women by way of predominance, like the pronoun of "aqradu," and the prepositional phrase is the deputy subject. It was said: it is the pronoun of the charity or the pronoun of the loan, with an elided genitive, i.e., the reward of the charity or the reward of the loan is multiplied for them. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amir read "yudda'afu" with the 'ayn doubled, and it was read "yudaa'ifu" in the active voice, i.e., Allah, Mighty and Majestic, multiplies for them the reward of that. ﴿And for them is a noble reward﴾. The discussion of it has already passed.

[Page 183]

﴿Those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾: He has already explained the manner of their belief at the end of Surat al-Baqarah. The relative pronoun (al-mawsul) is the first subject (mubtada' awwal). His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Ulaika﴾ ("those"), is the second subject, and it is a demonstrative referring back to the relative pronoun, carrying the sense of distance that has been mentioned many times before. His saying, Glorified is He, ﴿hum﴾ ("they"), is the third subject. His saying, Mighty and Majestic is He, ﴿al-siddiqun wa-al-shuhada'﴾ ("the truthful and the martyrs"), is the predicate of the third subject. The whole clause is the predicate of the second subject, and the second subject together with its predicate is the predicate of the first. Alternatively, ﴿hum﴾ is a separating pronoun (damir al-fasl), and what follows it is the predicate of the second subject. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿'inda rabbihim﴾ ("with their Lord"), is, according to what has been said, connected to the state of being established that the sentence implies. That is: ﴿Ulaika 'inda rabbihim﴾, that is, they are with their Lord, Mighty and Majestic, and in His judgment and knowledge, Glorified is He, ﴿hum al-siddiqun wa-al-shuhada'﴾, they are the truthful and the martyrs.

The meaning is that those, in the judgment of Allah Exalted, hold the rank of the truthful and the martyrs who are renowned for their lofty station and elevated position. These are the ones who were foremost in affirming the truth, who were firmly established in it, and who were martyred in the way of Allah, Majestic in His majesty. Whoever is killed while striving in His way is called a shahid (martyr), because Allah, Glorified is He, and His angels, upon them be peace, bear witness (shuhud) to his entry into Paradise. It has also been said that he is called so because he is alive and has not died, as though he were shahid, meaning present. It has also been said that it is because the angels of mercy witness him. It has been said that it is because he witnessed what Allah Exalted has prepared for him of honor. It has been said other than this. So the word is either fa'il in the sense of fa'il (active) or in the sense of maf'ul (passive), according to the differing interpretations.

His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿lahum ajruhum wa-nuruhum﴾ ("for them is their reward and their light"), is a second predicate of the relative pronoun, as it is a sentence consisting of a subject and predicate. Or, ﴿lahum﴾ is the predicate, and what follows it is raised by it as the agent (fa'iliyyah), and the pronoun in ﴿lahum﴾ refers to the relative pronoun. The last two pronouns refer to the truthful and the martyrs. The purpose is to state the fruits of the perfect qualities by which they have been described. That is: those, for them is the like of the reward of the truthful and the martyrs and their light, who are known for the utmost perfection and for a rare attainment. The particle of comparison has been omitted to draw attention to the strength of the resemblance and to its reaching the degree of identity, just as it was done at the beginning when it was said, ﴿Ulaika hum al-siddiqun wa-al-shuhada'﴾. The resemblance is not between what belongs to the first group of reward and light and what belongs to the last two groups in full, but rather between the full amount belonging to the first group of basic reward and multiplication, and what belongs to the last two of the basic amount without multiplication. Multiplication is what distinguishes the last two groups over the first group. It may also be that no figurative comparison is considered in the speech at all, and it remains on its apparent meaning. All the pronouns refer to the relative pronoun, that is: those are the ones who exceed in truthfulness, in that they believed and affirmed all the reports of Allah Exalted and the reports of His messengers, upon them be prayers and peace, and who bear witness to Allah, Glorified is He, to His oneness and all the other attributes of perfection. For them, in a manner befitting them, is the reward and the light that were promised to them.

Some have said: He described them with witnessing because they are witnesses over mankind, as His saying, Exalted is He, expresses: ﴿And thus We have made you a middle nation, that you may be witnesses over mankind﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143]. Then ﴿'inda rabbihim﴾ is connected to the martyrs, and the meaning is "and the witnesses over mankind on the Day of Resurrection." It has also been permitted for it to be connected to the martyrs according to the first interpretation, in the sense of those who witnessed an increase of honor through being killed in the way of Allah Exalted on the Day of Resurrection, or in the enclosure of His mercy, Mighty and Majestic, or something similar. Numerous reports support the view that the martyrs are coordinated with the truthful.

Ibn Jarir reported from al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: «Indeed, the believers of my community are martyrs.» Then the Prophet (ﷺ) recited: ﴿Those who believe in Allah and His messengers, those are the truthful and the martyrs with their Lord﴾.

Ibn Abi Hatim reported from Abu Hurayrah that he once said to a people sitting with him: "All of you are truthful and martyrs." He was asked: "What do you say, O Abu Hurayrah?" He said: "Recite: ﴿Those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾ to the end of the verse."

'Abd al-Razzaq and 'Abd ibn Humayd reported from Mujahid, who said: "Every believer is truthful and a martyr," and then he recited the verse.

'Abd ibn Humayd reported something similar from 'Amr ibn Maymun.

Ibn Hibban reported from 'Amr ibn Murrah al-Juhani, who said: "A man came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, what do you think if I testify that there is no god but Allah and that you are the Messenger of Allah, and I pray the five prayers, pay the zakat, fast Ramadan and stand in its night prayer, then to which group do I belong?' He said: 'You are among the truthful and the martyrs.'"

It is appropriate that ﴿Those who believe﴾ be understood as referring to those for whom belief is of worth, as in the case mentioned, which is attained only by performing acts of obedience that are regarded as worthwhile. Otherwise, it is far-fetched that a believer who is immersed in desires and heedless of acts of obedience should be truthful or a martyr.

[Page 184]

This is supported by the report from 'Umar, may Allah be pleased with him: «What is wrong with you, when you see a man tearing into the honor of people, that you do not rebuke him?» They said: "We fear his tongue." He said: "That is more likely to prevent you from being witnesses." Ibn al-Athir said: That is, if you do not do this, you will not be among the martyrs who will bear witness on the Day of Resurrection against the nations that denied their prophets. Similarly, the Prophet's saying, upon him be prayers and peace: «Those who curse excessively will not be witnesses,» according to one of two opinions concerning it.

In some reports there is something whose apparent meaning is the intention of a select group of the believers. Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: «Whoever flees with his religion from land to land, fearing trials for his self and his religion, is written with Allah as a truthful one. When he dies, Allah takes him as a martyr.» Then he recited this verse: ﴿Those who believe in Allah and His messengers, those are the truthful and the martyrs﴾, and then he said: "This applies to them." Then he said: "Those who flee with their religion from land to land on the Day of Resurrection will be with 'Isa ibn Maryam in his rank in Paradise."

It is permissible that his saying, "This applies to them," means that it is true of them and that they are included in it at the first level of inclusion. It is said that the Prophet's saying, upon him be prayers and peace: «with 'Isa in his rank» means "with him in a rank like his," and the resemblance is understood in the manner already mentioned. If the report is sound, it supports the first interpretation of the verse.

It is reported from al-Dahhak that it was revealed concerning eight men who preceded the people of the earth in their time to Islam. They were Abu Bakr, 'Umar, 'Uthman, 'Ali, Hamzah, Talhah, al-Zubayr, Sa'd and Zayd, may Allah be pleased with them all. This does not harm the generality of the verse, as is not hidden. It has also been said that al-Shuhada' is the subject and ﴿'inda rabbihim﴾ is its predicate. It has also been said that the predicate is ﴿lahum ajruhum﴾, and the statement is complete at His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿al-siddiqun﴾ ("the truthful").

Ibn Jarir reported this from Ibn 'Abbas and al-Dahhak, who both said: ﴿Those who believe in Allah and His messengers, those are the truthful﴾ is a separate clause; He named them truthful. Then He said: ﴿And the martyrs, with their Lord, for them is their reward and their light﴾.

A group reported from Masruq something that agrees with this, and they differed about the intended meaning of the martyrs according to this view. It was said: the martyrs are those who die in the way of Allah Exalted. This is reported from Muqatil ibn Sulayman. It was also said: the prophets, upon them be peace, who bear witness for their nations against them. This is reported from Masruq and Muqatil ibn Hayyan, and it was preferred by al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj. Abu Hayyan claimed that the apparent meaning is that the martyrs are the subject and what follows is the predicate. Whoever is fair knows that this is not as he said, and that what the eloquence of the noble composition requires is what has preceded. Then, according to all the possible interpretations, the light is in its literal sense. It is also reported from Mujahid and others that it is a figure of speech for guidance, honor and glad tidings.

﴿And those who disbelieve and deny Our signs﴾: that is, all of them, in their various kinds. It is a reference to their disbelief in all the messengers, upon them be peace. ﴿Those﴾: those who are described with that ugly attribute. ﴿Are the companions of the Blazing Fire﴾, in such a way that they never depart from it forever. [Al-Hadid: 20–29]

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 57, verse 20:

﴿Know that the life of this world is only play and amusement, adornment and boasting among yourselves, and competition in wealth and children.﴾ After mentioning the condition of the two groups in the Hereafter, He explained the condition of the life in which the second group found contentment. It is indicated that it is among the trivial matters which sensible people do not rely upon, let alone find contentment in. It is described as "play," which has no fruit except fatigue. ("Amusement") that distracts a person from what concerns and matters to him. ("Adornment") from which no inherent nobility is gained, such as fine clothing, splendid mounts, and lofty dwellings. ("Boasting") in lineages and decayed bones. ("Competition") in number and equipment. Al-Sulami read "wa-tafakhara baynikum" with the genitive construction. Then it is indicated that, despite all this, it is swift to vanish and near to perish, by His saying, glorified is He: ﴿like the likeness of rain﴾, that is, rainfall, ﴿which pleases the disbelievers﴾, that is, delights them, ﴿with its vegetation﴾, that is, the plant that results from it. The "disbelievers" here may be either the farmers, according to what is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud, because they "cover" (yakfuruna), that is, they conceal the seed in the earth. The reason for singling them out is clear. Or they may be the disbelievers in Allah, glorified is He. The reason for singling them out is that they are more pleased with the adornment of this world, for when the believer sees something that pleases him, his thought moves to the power of its Creator, mighty and majestic is He, and so he is pleased by that power. For this reason Abu Nuwas said about the narcissus:

Eyes of silver, gazing outward, whose edges are pure gold,
upon stalks of emerald, bearing witness ∗∗∗ that Allah has no partner.

But the disbelievers' thought does not go beyond what they perceive, so they are wholly absorbed in admiration. ﴿Then it dries up﴾, that is, it moves toward the utmost extent possible for it. It was said: that is, it withers after its greenness and freshness. ﴿Then you see it﴾, O you to whom sight is possible, ﴿yellowed﴾ after you had seen it fresh and gleaming. It is read "muṣfārran." He did not say "fa-yaṣfarru" (and it becomes yellow). It was said: this is to signal that its yellowing is not concurrent with its drying up, and that what follows from it is that he sees it in this state. It was also said: this is to indicate that this becomes evident to everyone. ﴿Then it becomes debris﴾, crumbled and shattered from dryness. The place of the kaf (like) is said to be in the accusative as a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ("play"), since it carries the sense of a description. It was also said to be in the nominative, as a second predicate for "the life of this world," with an elided genitive, meaning: the likeness of the life is like the likeness of etc. Since this implies the comparison of all the many years in it to the duration of the growth of a single rainfall, which passes away and perishes in less than a year, there is an indication of the swiftness of its passing and the nearness of its perishing. After explaining the insignificance of the affair of this world, to make one averse to it and to repel one from devotion to it, He pointed to the magnificence of the affair of the Hereafter and the greatness of its pleasures and pains, to encourage the attainment of its enduring bliss and to warn against its painful punishment. Glorified is He placed the mention of punishment first, saying, exalted is He: ﴿And in the Hereafter there is severe punishment﴾, because it is one of the results of absorption in what has been detailed of the states of the life of this world. ﴿And forgiveness﴾, great, ﴿from Allah, and approval﴾, great, whose measure cannot be estimated. The contrasting of severe punishment with two things indicates the predominance of mercy, and that it is of the type of "no hardship will overcome two eases."

Omitting to describe the punishment as being from Allah, while describing what follows it with that, also indicates the predominance of the latter, and is a sign that goodness is the primary intended aim. ﴿And the life of this world is nothing but the enjoyment of delusion﴾ for whoever finds contentment in it and does not make it a means to the Hereafter and a mount to its bliss. It is narrated from Sa'id ibn Jubayr: "The world is the enjoyment of delusion" if it distracts you from seeking the Hereafter. As for when it calls you to seeking the approval of Allah, exalted is He, and seeking the Hereafter, then it is an excellent enjoyment and an excellent means.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 57, verse 21:

﴿Hasten to forgiveness﴾ meaning: hasten with the haste of those who outstrip their rivals on the racecourse, toward the means of a great forgiveness ﴿from your Lord﴾. The speech here is metaphorical (isti'arah) or a loose metonymy (majaz mursal), using the expression for its necessary meaning. This is necessary because what is required is that one who performs what is a cause of forgiveness and entry into Paradise should hasten to it, not that he should do it or be characterized by it ahead of another. It has also been said: the intended meaning is "Outstrip the Angel of Death before he cuts you off from the deeds that lead to what has been mentioned by death." And it has been said: "Outstrip Iblis before he turns you away from that by his deception and trickery." But this, as you see, is weak.

The intended meaning of those means (asbab) is the righteous deeds in their various kinds. It is reported from 'Ali, may Allah ennoble his face, that he said concerning the verse: "Be the first to enter the mosque and the last to leave it." 'Abd Allah said: "Be in the front row of the battle line." Anas said: "Witness the opening takbir (takbir al-ihram) with the imam." All of these are by way of example (tamthil). This command has been cited as evidence that praying at the beginning of its time is better than delaying it.

﴿and a Garden whose breadth is like the breadth of heaven and earth﴾, meaning: like their breadth all together, were one of them joined to the other.
Page 186
Since breadth, which is the shorter of the two dimensions, is described as vast, this indicates that its length is vast by even greater reason. Thus restricting the description to breadth is more eloquent than mentioning length along with it. It has also been said: the intended meaning of "breadth" is spaciousness (al-basṭah), and for this reason it is attributed to supplication and the like, which are not among things having dimensions. Another opinion was given earlier in interpreting a parallel verse in Surah Al 'Imran. The mention of forgiveness before Paradise is due to the precedence of clearing (takhliyah) over adorning (tahliyah).

﴿It has been prepared for those who believe in Allah and His messengers﴾, meaning: it has been made ready for them. From this, it has been used as evidence that Paradise already exists now, because of His words "it has been prepared" in the past tense. The interpretation (ta'wil) is contrary to the apparent meaning, and it has been explicitly stated otherwise in sound hadiths. The full discussion belongs to the science of kalam. It has also been used as evidence that faith alone is sufficient for deserving Paradise, since it is mentioned alone within the scope of what suggests the cause of its preparation. Yet bringing deeds into faith, when faith is transitively governed by "bi", is not accepted, so they said. And if by "those who believe" is meant those mentioned who have a degree of faith that is counted, and it has been said that this degree is not attained without righteous deeds, as you heard from us shortly before, then the second argument is generally undermined, as is not hidden.

Al-Nisaburi mentioned, regarding the wording here, "sabiqu" (outstrip) and in the verse of Al 'Imran "sari'u" (hasten), and regarding "as the heaven" here versus "the heavens" there, and "ka-'ardi" (like the breadth) here versus "'ardu" (breadth) without the particle of comparison there, a discussion based on the premise that the intended meaning of "the God-fearing" there is "the foremost who are brought near," and the meaning of "those who believe" here is those who are below those. So reflect.

﴿That﴾, meaning: what has been promised of forgiveness and Paradise, ﴿is the bounty of Allah﴾, His gift which is not obligatory upon Him, ﴿He gives it to whomever He wills﴾, giving it, ﴿and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾. Thus it is far from Him, Mighty and Majestic, to bestow this bounty upon whomever He wills, however great his station may be. The sentence is therefore a concluding affirmation (tadhyil) establishing what it concludes.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 57, verse 22:

﴿No calamity befalls﴾ meaning: no misfortune, whatever misfortune it may be. Its origin is in archery (al-ramya), from "the arrow struck" (aṣāba al-sahm) when it reached the target accurately. The word was then specialized for it.

Some scholars claimed that it is a general term in language for both evil and good, but in customary usage it is specific to evil. The particle *min* (in *min muṣība*) is added for emphasis. *Aṣāba* is used for evil, as here, and for good, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if a bounty from Allah reaches you﴾ [al-Nisa, 73]. Some have mentioned that it is used for good by analogy with *al-ṣawb* (the rain), and for evil by analogy with the striking of an arrow (*iṣābat al-sahm*). Both return to one root. Making the verb masculine in such a case is permissible, as is making it feminine. On this basis is His saying, exalted is He: *mā* (*tasbiqu min ummatin ajalahā*) [al-Hijr, 5; al-Mu'minun, 43], meaning: no nation can precede its term.

The statement is general, covering all evils. That is, "a misfortune, whatever misfortune it may be." ﴿in the earth﴾, such as drought, blight on crops and fruits, earthquakes and others; ﴿nor in yourselves﴾, such as sickness and injury, like a wound or a fracture; ﴿except that it is in a Book﴾, i.e., except that it is written and recorded in the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfuz). It has been said: in the knowledge of Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

﴿before We bring it into being﴾, i.e., before We create it. The pronoun, according to what is related from Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Hasan and a group, refers to the souls (*al-anfus*). It has been said that it refers to the earth. Abu Hayyan preferred that it refers to the misfortune, since that is what is being spoken of. The mention of the earth and the souls is only by way of mentioning their place. Al-Mahdawi mentioned that it may refer to all that has been mentioned. A group said: it refers to the creatures, even though they have not been mentioned. It has also been said that by "misfortune" here is meant events, good and bad, but this goes against the usual use of the word *muṣība*. Still, what follows gives some support to it. In any case, ﴿in the earth﴾ is attached to something omitted, either in the nominative or the genitive position, as a qualifier of *muṣība*, either by its position or by its wording. It is also permitted that it be an adverbial complement of *aṣāba* or of *muṣība*.

It has been said: the misfortune was restricted to being in the earth and in the souls because all unrestricted events are not written in the Tablet, since they are not finite, whereas the Tablet is finite, and it cannot be a container for what is infinite. For this reason it is reported: "The pen has dried with what will be until the Day of Resurrection."

[Page 187]

In the verse there is another specification: He, glorified is He, did not mention the conditions of the people of the heavens, since the purpose does not concern that, and misfortunes among them are few; hardly anything befalls them except the misfortune of death. What was mentioned as the reason for the first specification does not hold if by the Book is meant His knowledge, glorified is He. It has also been said that the writing of events in it is in the manner of their being written in the Great Qur'an, on the basis of what they say: there is nothing that cannot be extracted from it, even the names of kings, their armies, and what happens among them. If it were said, regarding its reason, that what best suits what preceded of the description of the present life is only the mention of worldly misfortunes, and for this reason they alone were singled out for mention, it would be complete and unrestricted.

﴿Indeed, that﴾, i.e., recording them in a Book, ﴿for Allah﴾, not for anyone other than Him, glorified is He, ﴿is easy﴾, because He, exalted is He, is free of needing preparation or time for it. If by that is meant that they are realized in His knowledge, exalted is His glory, then it is easy because it is one of the requirements of His essence, Mighty and Majestic.

In the verse there is a refutation of Hisham ibn al-Hakam, who claimed that He, glorified is He, does not know events before they occur. In al-Iklil it is said that the verse is also a refutation of the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination). This is also reported in a raised hadith. al-Daylami related from Sulaym ibn Jabir al-Juhani, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "A gate of predestination will be opened for my community at the end of time, which nothing can close. What suffices you from it is to meet it with this verse: ﴿No calamity befalls…﴾" to the end of the verse.

Imam Ahmad and al-Hakim related, and he authenticated it, from Abu Hassan that two men entered upon 'A'isha, may Allah be pleased with her, and said: "Abu Hurayra narrates that the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: 'Ill omen (al-tiyara) is only in the woman, the animal and the house.'" She said: "By Him who revealed the Qur'an to Abu al-Qasim (ﷺ), he did not say it this way. Rather, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say: 'The people of the Jahiliyya used to say: ill omen is only in the woman, the animal and the house.'" Then she recited: ﴿No calamity befalls…﴾ to the end of the verse.

﴿So that you do not despair﴾, i.e., We have informed you of this so that you do not grieve ﴿over what has escaped you﴾ of the blessings of this world, ﴿nor exult over what He has given you﴾, i.e., what Allah the Exalted has bestowed upon you of it. For whoever knows that everything is predestined, that what has been decreed to be lost will be lost and what has been decreed to arrive will inevitably arrive, his anxiety over what has passed will not be great, nor his joy over what is coming. He knows that all of it is predestined, even though the text mentioned earlier was about calamities and not blessings or other things, because no one makes a distinction between them. The noble text does not rely on one part to indicate the other, as some have imagined. Yes, if "calamity" is taken to mean events, whether good or evil, then the matter of knowledge becomes clearer, as is not hidden. The parallel between the two verbs in the two relative clauses has been left out, since they are not attributed to the same thing. Rather, the first is attributed to the pronoun of the relative clause, and the second to His pronoun, the Exalted, because loss and non-existence are intrinsic to things. If they were left to themselves, they would not remain, unlike their coming into being and their continuation, which necessarily require their attribution to Him, the Mighty and Majestic, as has been established in its proper place. Upon this is the saying of the poet:

*So do not let your question about the past be "why did it pass?"*
*Turn instead to what remains, and ask it "why did it remain?"*

Similar to this is the reading of Abd Allah: ﴿ʾūtītum﴾ in the passive voice, meaning "you were given." Abu 'Amr read ﴿ʾatākum﴾ from ʾityān (coming), meaning "it came to you." According to this reading, the parallel between the two verbs also holds. The intended meaning is the negation of grief that leads a person to a state that distracts him from patience, submission to the command of Allah the Exalted, and hope for the reward of the patient, and the negation of joy that is arrogant and distracts from gratitude. As for grief that a person almost inevitably experiences, together with submission, and joy in the blessing of Allah the Exalted, acknowledging it with gratitude, there is no harm in these two.

A group, including al-Hakim, who authenticated it, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said regarding the verse: "No one is free of grief and joy, but whoever is struck by a calamity makes it patience, and whoever receives good makes it gratitude."

And His saying, the Exalted:

Page 188

﴿Allah does not love every arrogant boaster﴾. This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) indicating that the blameworthy joy is that which produces pride and conceit. The *mukhtāl* is one who is arrogant because of an imagined virtue that appears to him from his own self, and the *fakhūr* is one who boasts about things outside a person, such as wealth and status.

Some scholars mentioned that *ikhtiyāl* (conceit) relates to the act, while *fakhr* (boasting) relates to it and to other things. The meaning of "does not love" is "dislikes," since there is no intermediate state between love and dislike with regard to Him, the Mighty and Majestic. Such statements are interpreted (ta'wil, i.e., explained beyond their apparent meaning) as reward and punishment. The method of the early generations (al-Salaf) is to leave interpretation aside while affirming His transcendence. Saying "He does not love every arrogant person" does not mean "He does not love each one of them individually," as opposed to "He does not love some but loves others." This is refuted by the statement of Shaykh 'Abd al-Qahir, who said: "When we reflect, we find that placing each one within the scope of negation is only appropriate where it is meant that some were and some were not." Yes, this ruling is generally applicable (aktharī) but not universal (kullī).

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who are stingy and enjoin stinginess upon people﴾ is a *badal* (substitute) for ﴿every arrogant boaster﴾, a *badal kull min kull* (a substitute in which the whole replaces the whole), for the one who is proud of his wealth is generally stingy with it and orders others to do the same. The apparent meaning is that they literally enjoin it, though it has been said: they were exemplars, so it is as if they enjoin it. Or it is the predicate of a deleted subject, meaning: they are those who, etc. Or it is a subject whose predicate is deleted, its estimate being: they turn away from spending, which is free of need of Allah, Mighty and Majestic. This is indicated by His saying, Exalted: ﴿Whoever turns away, then indeed Allah is the Free of need, the Praiseworthy﴾, for its meaning is: whoever turns away from spending, then indeed Allah, glorified is He, is free of need of it and of its spending, praiseworthy in His essence. Turning away from thanking Him by drawing near to Him with some of His blessings does not harm Him, may His majesty be exalted. It has been said: its estimate is "unneeded by them," or "they are promised punishment," or "they are blamed."

It is permissible that it be in the accusative position, with the implied sense of "I mean" (*a'ni*), or that it is an adjective (*na't*) of ﴿every arrogant boaster﴾, since it is somewhat specified, so describing it with a definite is acceptable. This is not sound. Ibn 'Atiyya said: the permissibility of such a construction is the view of al-Akhfash. It is not hidden what the sentence contains of an indication of threat for the one who turns away.

Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿fa-inna Allaha al-Ghaniyy﴾ with the omission of *huwa*, and so it is in the codices of Medina and Syria. In the other reading it is a *damir al-fasl* (pronoun of separation). Abu 'Ali said: it is not good for it to be a subject, for otherwise, why would it not be permissible to delete it in the second reading? What follows it is suitable to be a predicate, so there would be no evidence for deletion. This is based on the requirement that the two readings agree in grammatical case, and this requirement is not binding.

**Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 57, verse 25:**

﴿We indeed sent Our messengers﴾, that is, from among the children of Adam, as is the apparent meaning, ﴿with clear proofs﴾, that is, with arguments (*hujaj*) and miracles (*mu'jizat*, signs that exceed human capacity). ﴿And We sent down with them the Book﴾, that is, the category of Book, which encompasses all of them. The adverbial phrase (*zarf*) is a presumed circumstantial clause (*hal muqaddarah*) from it, according to what Abu Hayyan said. It was also said that it means "accompanying," with the sending down being treated as accompaniment. ﴿And the balance﴾, the instrument known among people, as Ibn Zayd and others said. Its sending down is the sending down of its causes, though this is remote. The commanding of people to adopt it is accompanied by teaching them how to use it.

﴿So that people may uphold justice﴾ is the purpose (*'illah*) for the sending down of the Book and the balance. Upholding justice, that is, with equity, includes making things even in matters of dealing, through the use of the balance, and in matters of the return (*ma'ad*), through following the Book. It is a comprehensive term that includes everything one should be characterized by in this life and the next.

﴿And We sent down iron﴾. Al-Hasan said: that is, We created it, like His words, exalted is He: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6]. This interpretation is concomitant with the thing, for every created thing is "sent down" in the sense of its being recorded in the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh*) and its being decreed as existing wherever it is recorded.

Qutrub said: We made it ready for you and bestowed it upon you as a favour, from the expression *nazala al-dayf* (the guest alighted). ﴿In it is severe might﴾, that is, severe punishment, ﴿because instruments of war are made from it. This points to the need of the Book and the balance for one who stands by the sword, so that upholding justice may be realized, for injustice is among the dispositions of souls. His words, exalted is He: ﴿and benefits for people﴾, that is, in their livelihoods and their welfare, since there is no craft except that...

[Page 189]

...and iron, or what is worked to make its tools, is an allusion to the fact that upholding justice, just as it requires a restraining force (*al-wazi'*), which is the one who stands by the sword, also requires that by which social coexistence is sustained. Those who carry out this task are also needed so that civilization (*al-tamaddun*), which the human species needs, may be completed, and so that upholding justice may be completed. How could it not be, since it also includes what concerns a person alone? The clause introduced by the adverbial phrase is in the place of a circumstantial clause (*hal*). His words, glorified is He: ﴿and so that Allah may know who supports Him and His messengers﴾ are conjoined (*'atf*) to an omitted element indicated by the context, or they form a circumstantial clause, because it contains the sense of purpose. That is: so that it may benefit them, and so that Allah, exalted is He, may have a knowledge by which reward is connected to whoever supports Him and His messengers by using instruments of war made of iron in striving against His enemies. The omission indicates that the second is the thing sought for its own sake and the first is a preliminary to it. It is also permitted that it be connected to a postponed omitted element, with the waw being parenthetical, meaning: "and so that He may know," etc., [He] sent it down; or it may be a preposed element with the waw being conjunctive and the clause conjoined to what precedes it, the conjoined element having been omitted and its complement placed in its stead. His words, exalted is He: ﴿unseen﴾ are a circumstantial clause from the subject of "supports," or from its object, meaning: unseen from them, or they being unseen from Him. His words, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿Indeed Allah is strong, mighty﴾ are a concluding parenthetical clause (*i'tiradh tadhyili*) brought to establish the truth and to alert that the imposition of striving on them and their exposure to fighting is not for any need of His, glorified is He, in exalting His word and manifesting His religion, but rather it is so that they may benefit from it and attain reward through obeying the command concerning it. Otherwise, He, exalted and high is He, is free of them, through His power and might, in everything He wills.

This is what is said. Al-Zamakhshari, however, held that by "the messengers" is meant the messengers of the angels, peace be upon them, meaning: We sent them to the prophets, peace be upon them. He explained "the clear proofs" as we explained it, on the basis that the angels are sent with miracles just as they are sent with proofs, so that they might inform that these are miracles. Otherwise, the apparent meaning would have been to limit it to proofs. The sending down of the Book, that is, the revelation, along with those messengers is apparent. The sending down of the balance in the sense of the instrument is, according to him, in its literal sense. He said: "It is narrated that Gabriel, peace be upon him, came down with the balance and gave it to Noah, peace be upon him, and said: Command your people to weigh with it." Many explained it as justice. As for Ibn Abbas's statement regarding the sending down of iron: there descended with Adam, peace be upon him, the *mi'qa'a* (a hammer-like tool), the *sindan* (anvil), and the two tongs (*kalbatan*). It is also narrated that there descended with him the *murr* and the *mis'hah* (a spade). It was also said: there descended with him five iron items: the anvil, the two tongs, the needle, the hammer, and the *mi'qa'a*. The last was explained as the *mis'an* (whetstone), and it may mean a hammer or a large one of them. It was also said: that with which a millstone is sharpened. In a hadith of Ibn Abbas: Adam, peace be upon him, descended from Paradise with the *basinah*, which are the tools of craftsmen. It was also said: a plough-share, and it is not purely Arabic. And Allah knows best.

Abu Hayyan regarded as preponderant that "so that people may uphold justice" is the purpose only for the sending down of the balance, though what we have mentioned is permissible, and it is the preferable view in my opinion.

And His saying, ﴿Indeed, We sent Noah and Abraham﴾, is a kind of detailed explanation (*tafsil*) of what was stated in summary (*ijmal*) in His saying, ﴿Indeed, We sent Our messengers﴾. The repetition of the oath serves to show greater care for the matter, meaning: By Allah, We certainly sent Noah and Abraham.

﴿And We placed in their offspring prophethood and the Scripture﴾, by making them prophets and by revealing the books to them. Ibn 'Abbas said: "The Scripture" means writing with the pen. In the codex of 'Abdullah (*Mushaf* of Ibn Mas'ud), the word *al-nubuwwa* (prophethood) is written with a *ya'* instead of a *waw*. ﴿So among them is one who is guided﴾, meaning among the offspring. It was also said: meaning among those to whom the messengers were sent, which is implied by the mention of sending and of messengers. ﴿But many of them are transgressors﴾, meaning they have departed from the straight path.

He did not say "and many of them are astray" (*dall*), although it would be more apparent in contrast. The wording of the noble text is more eloquent in censure, because departing from the straight path after having reached it and become established upon it is more emphatic than going astray from it in the first place. It also signifies that the people of misguidance dominate over others.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 57, verse 27 (part 1 of 2):

﴿Then We sent, following in their footsteps, Our messengers﴾: that is, We sent after them one messenger after another. The origin of *taqfiyah* (following up, sending in succession) is placing something behind the nape of the neck. The pronoun in *athariham* (their footsteps) refers to Noah and Abraham and those who were sent to their peoples. It was also said that it refers to the messengers who were contemporaries of the two of them, peace be upon them.

It was objected that if a messenger were a contemporary of Noah, he would either be sent to his own people, like Aaron with Moses, or to other people, like Lot with Abraham, peace be upon them both. The first possibility is not admissible, because it contradicts the facts, and the second is not either, since there were no people on earth other than Noah's. It was answered that this is an interpretation to account for the plural of the pronoun, and that Lot's being a contemporary of Abraham suffices for it. It was also said that the pronoun refers to the descendants (*dhurriyyah*). But this has a problem: the messengers who were followed up were themselves among the descendants, so if the pronoun referred to them, it would follow that they are other than them, or that the follower and the followed are one and the same. And restricting the pronoun's referent to the earliest of the descendants is contrary to the apparent meaning, without any indication that supports it.

﴿And We followed up with Jesus, son of Mary﴾: We made him come after them.

The sum of the meaning is: We sent one messenger after another until the sending reached Jesus, peace be upon him. ﴿And We gave him the Injil (Gospel)﴾ by revealing to him. It is not the one that is in the hands of the Christians today, I mean the one that contains the account of his birth and the fabricated account of his crucifixion. Al-Hasan read *al-Anjil* with a fatha on the hamzah. Abu al-Fath said: it is a pattern for which there is no parallel. Al-Zamakhshari said: its case is easier than that of *al-barṭil* (bribe), pronounced with a fatha on the ba', though the kasra is more common; it is a long stone, and its use for bribery is a later usage derived from it by a kind of metaphorical extension, because it is non-Arabic, whereas this (the word) is Arabic, and they play with non-Arabic words and do not hold them to their patterns. Some claimed that the word *Injil* is Arabic, from *najaltu* meaning "I extracted," because the rulings are extracted from it.

﴿And We placed in the hearts of those who followed him kindness and mercy﴾: that is, We created or made (so *fi qulubi* is in the position of the second object). In either case, what is meant is that We placed this in their hearts, so that they show kindness to one another and have mercy on one another. A parallel to this, concerning the companions of the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, is ﴿compassionate among themselves﴾ [al-Fath: 29]. *Ra'fah* is commonly understood as mercy, but some eminent scholars said: when it is mentioned alongside *rahmah*, *ra'fah* refers to what averts evil and repairs a rift, and *rahmah* refers to what brings about good. This is why you generally find *ra'fah* mentioned before *rahmah*, because averting harms is more important than bringing about benefits. It was also read as *ra'afah* on the pattern *fa'alah*, like *shaja'ah* (courage).

﴿And monasticism﴾: is in the accusative, governed by a verb understood, which the apparent verb explains: that is, "and they invented monasticism."

﴿They invented it﴾: this is the construction of *al-ishtighal* (the verb governing a pronoun referring back to the noun it precedes). It was objected that, as Ibn al-Shajari and Abu Hayyan said, this construction requires that the preceding noun be definite and capable of being the subject of a sentence, and that the noun mentioned be indefinite with no justification from the justifications for beginning with an indefinite noun. It was answered that, even granting this condition, the noun here is semantically qualified by what is understood from the tanwin of magnification, as was said regarding their saying: "An evil, it snarls at the one with fangs."

It may also be governed by the attribution implied in the sentence, as you will hear, God willing; or it may be in the accusative by coordination with what precedes it. The clause ﴿they invented it﴾ is in the position of a qualifier. The sentence then involves an elided genitive (*mudaf*), meaning: "and We placed in their hearts kindness, mercy, and love of an invented monasticism." Some scholars made it coordinated with what was mentioned without addressing the elision. And he said: monasticism is among the actions of servants, because it is the exaggeration of worship through ascetic discipline and withdrawal from people. Its original meaning is the act attributed to the monks (*ruhban*), and the monk is one who fears, on the pattern *fa'lan* from *rahiba*, like *khashyan* from *khashiya*. The actions of servants are related to God's making (*ja'l*), according to the people of truth, while being acquired by the servant at the same time. Al-Zamakhshari permitted the aforementioned coordination and interpreted *al-ja'l* (making) as enabling (*tawfiq*), as if it were said: "We enabled them to show mercy among themselves and to invent and originate monasticism," on the basis of his doctrine that monasticism is an act of the servant, created by him through his own choice. The benefit of *fi qulubi* (in their hearts) on this depiction is, as it is said, [...]. There is no hiding what this interpretation involves of departing from the apparent meaning. But in fairness, the coordination is not good without this interpretation, or without considering an elided genitive and putting the genitive's complement in its place, as previously explained, or without interpreting monasticism as something of the heart, such as excessive fear that necessitates extremism in worship. A kind of metaphorical usage is employed in *ibtada'uha* and what follows it, such as meaning the invention of its actions and effects; or a kind of *istikhdam* (a word used in two senses) is employed, by treating monasticism as having two meanings, excessive fear for example, and meaning by "We placed in their hearts monasticism" both the arduous devotional practices, such as renouncing the world and its desires, including women and others. And "they invented it" and what follows it is meant in the other sense. The reason for the interpretation is not Mu'tazilism, but rather that monasticism, in the sense of bodily actions, is not among the things placed in the heart like kindness and mercy. So reflect.

It was also read as *rahbaniyyatun* with a damma on the ra', which is a relative noun from *ruhban* with a damma. This (*ruhban*), as al-Raghib said, can be singular or plural, so the attribution is made by considering it as singular. Whoever thought that the damma form is specific to the plural said: since it became specific to a particular group, it is given the status of a proper noun, so its attribution is like what they said for *ansar* and *ansari* (Helper, pl. and sing. relative). Or the attribution to *ruhban* with the fatha, and the damma on the ra' in the attributive form, is one of the changes in relative nouns, as in *dahriyy* with a damma on the dal.

﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾: this is a new (independent) sentence. And His, the Glorified's, statement ﴿except seeking the pleasure of God﴾ is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*), meaning: We did not ourselves prescribe it for them at all, but they invented it and bound themselves to it, seeking the pleasure of God, the Exalted.

His statement ﴿but they did not observe it with the observance it deserved﴾: that is, they did not maintain it with the maintenance it deserved. This is a censure of them, since this is like a vow, which is a covenant with God, the Exalted, which must be observed, especially when it is intended for His pleasure, may He be glorified and exalted.

It has been used as evidence that whoever habitually performs a voluntary act, it becomes disliked for him to abandon it. It was also permitted that His statement ﴿We did not prescribe it﴾ etc. is another attribute of *rahbaniyyah*, and the negation is directed at the qualifier of the verb, not at the verb itself, as in the first case. And His, the Glorified's, statement ﴿except seeking﴾ etc. is a connected exception from the most general of the causes, meaning: We did not decree it for them, by making them invent it for any reason, except that they should seek by it the pleasure of God, the Exalted, and deserve the reward by it. And it necessarily follows that they should maintain it and observe it with the observance it deserves, but they did not observe it in that way.

The first interpretation is related from Qatadah and a group, and this one is related from Mujahid. There is no contradiction between ﴿they invented it﴾ and ﴿We did not prescribe it for them﴾ etc., since the first implies they were not commanded with it at all, while the second implies they were commanded with it for the sake of seeking the pleasure of God, the Exalted, as we pointed out regarding the meaning of ﴿We did not prescribe it for them except seeking﴾ etc. Some resolved the contradiction by saying: the command came after its invention, or *ibtada'uha* is interpreted as meaning that they were the first to do it after the command.

What supports what he mentioned first in the resolution is what Abu Dawud, Abu Ya'la, and al-Diya' transmitted from Anas: "The Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, said: Do not be strict with yourselves, lest it be made strict upon you. For a people were strict with themselves, so it was made strict upon them. Those are their remnants in the monasteries and the cloisters. A monasticism they invented; We did not prescribe it for them," meaning the verse.

The apparent reading is that the pronoun in ﴿but they did not observe it﴾ refers to those who invented monasticism, and the intent is the negation of observance by all of them, meaning: "they did not all observe it, but some of them did." The relative pronoun in what preceded does not refer to specific individuals by name, but rather to what encompasses the Christians up to the time of Islam. It does no harm to this that the origin of the invention came from a specific people, because its attribution is like the attribution in "The Banu Tamim killed Zayd," while the killer was some of them.

Al-Dahhak and others said: the pronoun in ﴿but they did not observe it﴾ refers to the opponents who came after the innovators. The first is more fitting with the grammatical construction. The intent of ﴿those of them who believed﴾ in His statement ﴿So We gave those of them who believed﴾ is those who believed with a sound faith, and this applies to those who lived in the time of the Prophet, upon whom be peace, and believed in him, peace be upon him. That is: "So We gave those of them who believed a sound faith, after observing their monasticism, their reward." ﴿Their reward﴾: that is, what is specifically due to them of reward, which is the reward for what preceded from them, and the reward for believing in him, peace be upon him. The intent is not those who remained observing monasticism until the time of the mission and did not believe, because observing it is pure futility and sheer disbelief, and it only has the consequence of reward. It is possible to say that those who did not observe monasticism as it deserved are those who denied him, peace be upon him.

Al-Zajjaj said: His statement ﴿but they did not observe it with the observance it deserved﴾ is of two kinds. One is that they fell short regarding what they had obligated themselves to. The other, which is the better, is that when the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace, was sent, they did not believe, so they were abandoners of obedience to God, and thus they did not observe that monasticism. The evidence for this is His statement ﴿So We gave those of them who believed﴾ etc. End of quote. So "those who believed" is understood as those among them who lived in his time, peace be upon him, and believed in the Prophet, may God bless him and grant him peace. And "the defiant ones" in His statement ﴿and many of them are defiant﴾ refers to those who did not believe in him, may God bless him and grant him peace. The consequence of understanding "those who believed" as you heard first is understanding it in the more general sense, encompassing those who had departed from following Jesus, peace be upon him, earlier. And understanding both groups as those who passed before, among those who observed the rights of monasticism before abrogation and those who neglected them at that time by trinitarianism, saying of unity (*al-ittihad*), seeking reputation, and similar things, without any reference to their faith in the Messenger of God, may God bless him and grant him peace, or their disbelief in him, is something the context does not support.

Among the reports that reject this view is a lengthy hadith narrated by a group including al-Hakim, who graded it sound, and al-Bayhaqi in *Shu'ab al-Iman*, through several chains from Ibn Mas'ud: "The people before us split into seventy-two sects. Three of them were saved, and all the rest perished. One sect confronted the kings and fought them in defense of the religion of God and of Jesus, son of Mary. Another sect had no strength to stand against the kings, so they remained among their people and called them to the religion of God and the religion of Jesus. The kings killed them and sawed them apart with saws. And another sect had no strength to stand against the kings or to remain with them, so they wandered off into the mountains and became monks (*tarahhabu*) there. These are the ones of whom God said: ﴿But monasticism they invented; We did not prescribe it for them; they sought only the pleasure of God; but they did not observe it with due observance. So We gave those of them who believed their reward, but many of them are defiantly disobedient﴾. Those who believed in Me and affirmed Me are the ones who believed, and those who denied Me and disbelieved in Me are the defiantly disobedient."

This report supports what al-Zajjaj preferred, and from it we also learn the reason for the innovation of monasticism. The verse does not indicate a blanket condemnation of innovation (*bid'ah*). What it apparently condemns is the failure to observe what they had committed themselves to.

As for the detailed discussion of *bid'ah*, Imam Muhyi al-Din al-Nawawi, in his commentary on *Sahih Muslim*, said: "The scholars said: *bid'ah* is of five categories: obligatory, recommended, forbidden, disliked, and permissible. Among the obligatory is learning the proofs of the theologians (*mutakallimun*) to refute the heretics (*al-malahidah*) and innovators and the like. Among the recommended is writing books of knowledge, building schools and hospices (*ribat*), and other such things. Among the permissible is indulgence in various kinds of food and other such things. The forbidden and the disliked are self-evident." From this it is known that the Prophet's saying (ﷺ), "Every innovation is misguidance," is one of the general statements that has been specified (*'amm makhsus*).

The author of *Jami' al-Usul* said: "Innovation by created beings, if it opposes what God Most High and His Messenger (ﷺ) commanded, then it falls under censure and denunciation. If it falls under the general scope of what God Most High and His Messenger (ﷺ) recommended and urged, then it falls under praise, even if no precedent for it existed, such as a kind of generosity, liberality, and doing good."

This is reinforced by the saying of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, may God be pleased with him, concerning the *tarawih* prayer: "What an excellent innovation this is!"

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 57, verse 28:

﴿O you who have believed﴾ Abu Hayyan preferred the view that the address is to those among his community (ﷺ) who believed, other than the People of the Book, and the reports support this. Al-Tabarani in al-Awsat related from Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Abi Hatim from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, both of whom said: "Forty of the companions of the Negus came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and they witnessed Uhud with him, and some of them were wounded, and none of them was killed. When they saw the need that the believers were in, they said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we are people of means, so permit us to bring our wealth to comfort the Muslims with it.' So Allah the Exalted revealed concerning them: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book before it, they believe in it﴾ up to His words, glorified is He: ﴿Those will be given their reward twice over, for what they endured patiently﴾ [al-Qasas: 52–54], and He made for them two rewards. When this verse was revealed, they said: 'O assembly of Muslims, as for whoever among us believed in your Book, he has two rewards, and whoever did not believe in your Book has a reward like your rewards.' So Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿O you who have believed﴾, the verse, meaning: as a rejoinder to them concerning their saying: 'and whoever did not believe in your Book has a reward like your rewards.'"

In al-Kashshaf: the one who said this was one of the People of the Book who had not believed, and they said it when they heard that verse, boasting of it over the Muslims. The meaning is: O you who have attributed to yourselves faith, ﴿fear Allah﴾, remain steadfast in His piety, the Mighty and Majestic, in what He has forbidden you.

﴿And believe in His Messenger﴾, and remain steadfast in faith in His Messenger whom He has sent to you, and he is Muhammad (ﷺ). In referring to him in this way there is what is not hidden of indication of the greatness of his station (peace be upon him). ﴿He will give you﴾ because of that.

﴿A double portion of His mercy﴾. Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: "Two times (ḍi'fayn) in the language of Abyssinia." Others said: "Two shares (naṣībayn)." The intended meaning is that He gives them two rewards like the believers among the People of the Book, as if it were said: He will give you what He promised those among the People of the Book who believed of the two rewards, because you are like them in believing in the earlier Messengers and in their Seal (ﷺ), upon all of them, and "do not make a distinction between any of His messengers."

Al-Raghib said: al-kifl is the portion in which there is sufficiency, as if one is made responsible for his affair. The two kifls are what is desired by His saying: ﴿Our Lord, give us good in this world and good in the Hereafter﴾ [al-Baqarah: 201], and there is no indication of restriction.

﴿And will make for you a light by which you will walk﴾ on the Day of Resurrection, and it is the light mentioned in His saying: ﴿Their light runs before them and on their right hands﴾ [al-Hadid: 12]. ﴿And will forgive you﴾ what has passed of you. ﴿And Allah is Forgiving, Merciful﴾, meaning: He is exceedingly abundant in forgiveness and mercy, so it is no wonder when He does what He does, glorified is He.

Commentary of al-Alusi (Ruh al-Ma'ani) on surah 57, verse 29:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so that the People of the Book may know that they have no power over any of the bounty of Allah﴾. It was said: it is connected to the meaning of the imperative sentence, which implies the sense of a condition, since the implied meaning is: "If you fear Allah and believe in His Messenger, He will give you such and such, so that..." etc. It was also said: it is connected to the three verbs preceding it by way of *tanazu'* (the grammatical dispute over a shared complement), or to an implied verb such as "He did that and informed them," and the like. The *lā* is extra, like its use in His saying: what ﴿prevented you from prostrating﴾ [al-A'raf: 12]. Its being extra when there is a clear indication is common. The *an* is the light form of the heavy *an* (*mukhaffafa min al-thaqila*), and its omitted noun is the pronoun of the People of the Book, i.e. "that they." It was also said: it is the pronoun of the matter (*ḍamir al-sha'n*), and what follows it is its predicate, and the clause is in the position of the accusative as the object of *ya'lama*, i.e. "so that the People of the Book who say: whoever among us believes in your Book has two rewards, and whoever does not believe in your Book has a reward like your rewards, may know that they do not obtain any of the bounty of Allah, of the two rewards or of anything else, and are not able to attain it, as long as they do not believe in Muhammad (ﷺ)." The essence of this is the information that their belief in their prophet does not benefit them at all unless they believe in the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace. Thus their saying: "whoever does not believe in your Book, he has a reward" is false.

[Page 194]

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Muqatil ibn Hayyan, who said: "When the verse ﴿Those will be given their reward twice, because they were patient﴾ [al-Qasas: 54] was revealed, the believers among the People of the Book boasted over the Companions of the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and said: 'We have two rewards, and you have one reward.' This was hard on his Companions, upon him be prayer and peace, so Allah the Exalted revealed: ﴿O you who have believed﴾..." etc., and He thereby made for them, glorified is He, two rewards like those of the believers among the People of the Book. Al-Tha'labi said: Allah the Exalted revealed ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah﴾, the verse, and He made for them two rewards and added to them a light. Then He said, glorified is He: ﴿so that [the People of the Book] may know﴾, etc. Its essence according to this is: so that they may know that they are not the owners of His bounty, mighty and majestic is He, so that they might withhold it from the believers and monopolize it to themselves to the exclusion of them.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and that the bounty is in the hand of Allah﴾ is coordinated with *an lā yaqdiruna* (that they have no power), and is included with it within the scope of knowing. His saying, glorified is He: ﴿He gives it to whom He wills﴾ is a second predicate of *anna*, or it is the predicate, and what precedes it is, according to what has been said, a necessary circumstantial clause (*ḥal lāzima*) or a resumptive statement (*isti'naf*). His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿and Allah is the Possessor of great bounty﴾ is a concluding interjection (*i'tiraḍ tadhyili*) that confirms the meaning of what precedes it.

Some have gone to the view that the address is to those among the People of the Book who are Jews and Christians who have believed, or to those among them who have not yet believed. The meaning then is: "O you who have believed in Moses and Jesus, peace be upon them both, believe in Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace," that is, "persist in belief in him," or "newly establish belief in him, upon him be prayer and peace, He will give you two portions of His mercy: a portion for your belief in the one in whom you believed first, and a portion for your belief in Muhammad, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, last, so that those among the People of the Book who have not believed may know that they do not obtain anything of what the believers among them obtain, and are not able to attain it, since they have not come with its condition, which is belief in His Messenger (ﷺ)." This is supported by what is in the Sahih of al-Bukhari: "Whoever has a slave-girl, and he teaches her and does well in teaching her, and disciplines her and does well in disciplining her, and frees her and marries her, he has two rewards. And whichever man of the People of the Book believes in his prophet and believes in me, he has two rewards. And whichever slave fulfills the right of Allah and the right of his masters, he has two rewards."

There is no difficulty in this regarding the Christians. For this reason it was said: the address is to them, because their religion was not abrogated before the emergence of the Muhammadan religion and their knowledge of it. So they are rewarded for acting by it, until it becomes obligatory for them to believe in the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. When they believe, they are also rewarded, so they have two rewards. Indeed, it may be objected with respect to others, because their religions were abrogated by the religion of Jesus, peace be upon him, and there is no reward for acting by an abrogated law. It is answered that it is not unlikely that they are rewarded for acting by their earlier religion even if it was abrogated, by the blessing of Islam.

Some have answered that the reward is for the very belief of that People of the Book in his prophet, even if his law was abrogated, since belief in every prophet is an obligation, whether his law was abrogated or not. It was also said: the *lā* in ﴿so that [they] may know﴾ is not extra, and the pronoun of *lā yaqdiruna* refers to the Prophet, may Allah bless him and grant him peace, and the believers. The meaning is: "We did what We did so that the People of the Book would not believe that the Prophet (ﷺ) and the believers who are with him have no power over any of the bounty of Allah, exalted is He, which is an expression for what they were given of the felicity of both abodes, and they do not attain it." Or: "that they, i.e. the Prophet, upon him be prayer and peace, and the believers, have no power, etc." On the basis that their not knowing that they have no power over that is a metonymy for their knowing that they have power over it. Then His saying, glorified is He: ﴿and that the bounty [is in the hand of Allah]﴾, etc., is coordinated with *an lā ya'lama* (that [they] may not know) and is included with it within the scope of the causal clause, not with *an lā yaqdira* (that they have no power). So it is as if it were said: "We did what We did so that they would not believe such and such, and because the bounty is in the hand of Allah." This would be a coordination of purpose upon purpose, according to the well-known view. Because this statement is strained and contradicts some readings (*qira'at*), most of the exegetes did not adopt it.

Khattab ibn Abdullah read *li-an lā ya'lama* with the explicit *an*. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, Ibn Abbas, Ikrimah, al-Jahdari, and Abdullah ibn Salama read *li-ya'lama*, with variation. Al-Jahdari also read *li-yayya'lama*, on the basis that its origin is *li-an ya'lama*. The hamza was changed to a *yā'* because of the kasra before it, and the *nūn* was assimilated into the *yā'* without nasalization (*ghunna*). Ibn Mujahid related from al-Hasan *layla*, like Layla, the name of a woman, *ya'lamu* with the nominative. It was explained that its origin is *li-an lā*, with the *fatḥa* on the preposition lām, which is a dialect, and upon it is the poet's saying:

"I wish to make myself forget her remembrance, but it is as if Layla has appeared to me on every path."

The hamza was deleted by *i'tibāt* (arbitrary deletion), and the *nūn* was assimilated into the lām, so it became *lal-lā*. The similar sounds accumulated and the pronunciation became heavy, so they replaced the assimilated lām with a *yā'*, in the manner of what they did in *qīrāṭ* and *dīnār*, since the original forms are *qirrāṭ* and *dinnār*, and they replaced one of the two identical letters in them with a *yā'* for ease. So it became *layla*. The verb is in the nominative because *an* here is the light form of the heavy *an*, not the one that puts the present verb in the subjunctive (*al-nāṣiba lil-muḍāri'*). Qutrub related from al-Hasan also *li-yalā* with a kasra on the lām, and its explanation is like the preceding, except that the kasra on the lām is according to the famous dialect for the preposition lām. From Ibn Abbas: *kay ya'lama* (so that he may know), and from him also: *li-kay-lā ya'lama* (so that he may not know). From Abdullah, Ibn Jubayr, and Ikrimah: *li-kay ya'lama* (so that he may know).

Abdullah read *an lā yaqdirū* with the nūn deleted, on the basis that *an* is the one that puts the present verb in the subjunctive. And Allah the Exalted knows best.

Among what the Sufis, may their secrets be sanctified, have mentioned regarding some of its verses: ﴿He is the First and the Last, and the Outward and the Inward﴾. They said: this is a reference to the oneness of His essence, glorified is He, which encompasses all things. And regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and He is with you wherever you are﴾, they said: it is a reference to the fact that they have no existence in all their stations without His existence, mighty and majestic is He. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿He causes the night to enter into the day and causes the day to enter into the night﴾ is a reference to the manifestation of the manifestation of majesty (*jalal*) within the manifestation of beauty (*jamal*), and vice versa. ﴿And spend from that in which He has made you successors﴾ is a reference to the perfected shaykhs (*mashayikh*) regarding the training of the disciples (*murīdīn*), by pouring forth what strengthens their readiness, from what Allah the Exalted has empowered them to possess of states and faculties.

He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Know that Allah gives life to the earth after its death﴾, so that the hard-hearted does not despair of His mercy, exalted is He, and abandon occupying himself with treating the dead heart. ﴿But they did not observe it with its proper observance﴾. The Sufis placed it in the chapter on observance (*ri'āya*) and divided it into the observance of deeds, states, and times. What they said about it returns, according to what has been said, to guarding it against committing any defect in it. ﴿O you who have believed, fear Allah and believe in His Messenger; He will give you a double portion of His mercy﴾, i.e. two portions: a portion of the knowledge of the active attributes, and a portion of the knowledge of the essential attributes. ﴿And He will make for you light﴾ from the light of His essence, mighty and majestic is He. According to what has been said, this is a reference to subsistence after annihilation (*baqā' ba'd al-fanā'*). It was also said: this light is a reference to the light of unveiling and witnessing. He, glorified is He, ordered its bestowal upon the believer on the basis of his piety and his belief in His greatest Messenger, may Allah bless him and grant him peace. It was also said: it is the light of beneficial knowledge, by which one is enabled to travel through the divine presences (*al-ḥaḍarāt al-ilāhiyya*), as its description indicates in His saying, mighty and majestic is He: ﴿by which you walk﴾. In some traditions: "Whoever acts by what he knows, Allah will teach him what he does not know." He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Fear Allah, and Allah will teach you﴾. All of that is in reality the bounty of Allah, exalted is He, and Allah, mighty and majestic is He, is the Possessor of great bounty. We ask Him, glorified is He, not to deprive us of His great bounty and His abundant kindness, and to keep us firm upon following His noble beloved, upon whom be from Allah the Exalted the best prayers and the most perfect peace.

Completed by the help and success of Allah the Exalted is the twenty-seventh part. It is followed by the twenty-eighth part, whose beginning is Surat al-Mujadila.
